body: Myth: cranking the batter head tighter always adds more crack. Actually over-tightening chokes the drum's tone and stresses the head instead of improving it.
Myth: any powered mic input works with any powered mic. Actually applying A-B (T-power) to a phantom-only microphone can damage it; they aren't interchangeable.
It's tempting to think an instrument input needs impedance matching. Actually it deliberately bridges with very high impedance so it won't load the pickup.
Myth: any studio monitor can just be built into a wall. Actually the speaker and soffit must be designed together, and the resulting bass boost needs re-EQ.
The myth: more overall loudness gives a sound more punch. Actually punch comes from transient contrast — a too-fast attack can remove it.
The myth: boosting the digital trim can fix a badly set analog preamp. Actually it works after conversion; it can't restore signal-to-noise lost before that.
Myth: a power regenerator just filters incoming AC like a conditioner. Actually it builds a brand-new sine wave from scratch, with no battery backup.
It's tempting to think every console and DAW uses the same pan law. In fact the center-attenuation amount varies by system, shifting level between them.
Common belief: a louder voice is just the same voice turned up evenly. Actually raised vocal effort shifts energy toward higher frequencies, not just level.
UCL and LDL sound like different tests. Actually they're near-synonyms for the same discomfort ceiling -- and it's not the same as MCL.
The myth: more watts means proportionally louder. Actually doubling amplifier power adds only about 3 dB — loudness doesn't scale directly with power.
Myth: more mantissa bits widen a float's dynamic range. Actually the exponent sets range - the significand only holds precision, not bit-depth resolution.
Common belief: mastering louder than a streaming target makes a track stand out. Actually the service turns it back down, so you only lose dynamics for nothing.
dBA and dBC readings are basically interchangeable? Not quite — dBC stays flat at low frequencies where dBA rolls off, revealing bass energy dBA hides.
A voice moving away seems barely quieter, even though far less sound reaches your ears. Your brain partly compensates for distance -- it's not perfect.
Myth: a quiet dBA reading means bass exposure is safe. A-weighting deliberately discounts low frequencies, so it can hide real low-end energy.
Popular belief: the space behind a mic's diaphragm has no effect on sound. Actually that rear chamber's size and damping shape its low-frequency response.
Myth: omnidirectional mics have proximity effect like directional ones. Actually true pressure omnis don't exhibit proximity effect at all.
Studio myth: a small speaker reproducing deep bass is actually radiating that note. Actually the ear rebuilds a missing fundamental from harmonics.
Myth: the ear responds to level in a straight line. The cochlea compresses -- boosting quiet sounds heavily and loud sounds far less, so both stay hearable.
Common belief: pushing every fader and plugin hot is fine as long as nothing clips yet. Actually summing many hot channels eats the master bus headroom fast.
Myth: crest factor and dynamic range are the same measurement. Actually crest factor is one signal's peak-to-RMS ratio, not the loud-to-quiet range.
Myth: soundcheck levels in an empty room are what a show needs. Actually a full crowd raises the ambient noise floor, overwhelming those empty-room settings.
Myth: any level meter shows the same thing. dBFS reads peaks, VU and PPM read differently smoothed averages, and LUFS reads perceived loudness.
Common belief: electrostatic headphones plug into a normal jack. Actually they need a dedicated energizer supplying the diaphragm's high polarizing voltage.
Myth: a cross-stick and a rimshot are the same technique. Actually a rimshot is a loud full hit, while a cross-stick is a soft, dry click with no drum tone.
Myth: weak bass in headphones means a weak driver. Actually a broken seal is usually the real cause — leakage kills low end before the driver's at fault.
A phase difference between channels is a polarity flip? Not quite — it's a frequency-dependent time offset between channels, not a simple inversion.
Widely believed: comparing to a reference track just means playing them back to back. Really, without level-matching, the louder mastered reference always wins.
Myth: a peak meter and a VU meter read the same number on identical audio. Actually peak meters catch fast transients while VU shows average level.
Commonly assumed: more predelay pushes a source farther back — but it's the opposite; longer predelay makes the source feel closer, mimicking a nearer room.
Myth: loudness normalization is the same as normalizing peaks to 0 dBFS. It targets integrated LUFS instead, with one gain change and no altered dynamics.
Myth: an SPL map's colors show the full-range loudness everywhere. Actually it's usually plotted for one stated frequency band, not the whole spectrum.
Myth: single-band compression only reacts to the frequency causing the problem. Actually one detector watches the whole signal — loud bass can dull everything.
Myth: if a sound is loud enough to hear, hearing works fine. Actually some hearing loss degrades how sounds are processed, so turning up volume doesn't fix it.
The myth: chamber reverb sounds like a large concert hall. Actually chambers are typically smaller and denser-sounding, with their own distinct character.
Myth: a bigger microphone diaphragm is always the better choice. Actually size trades sensitivity against off-axis, high-frequency accuracy.
Common belief: a higher sample rate always sounds better. Actually sample rate only sets bandwidth — dynamic range comes from bit depth.
Myth: white noise sounds tonally balanced. Actually equal energy per hertz piles up in the highs to our ears, so white noise actually sounds bright.
The myth: BS.1770 is a loudness target like -14 LUFS. Actually it's the measurement algorithm itself - rulebooks like EBU R128 set the targets on top.
Common belief: summing to mono just copies one channel. Actually it adds left and right together, so out-of-phase content can partly or fully cancel.
Myth: short-term loudness is gated like the integrated reading. Actually it's ungated, just a 3-second sliding window between momentary and full-program values.
Myth: a matrix output mainly pulls signal straight from channels. Actually it's usually fed from existing buses, its master scaling the whole combined output.
Myth: low THD guarantees low intermodulation distortion. Actually they probe different nonlinearities — a device can pass one test and still fail the other.
Myth: the same sound pressure level always sounds equally loud. Spread that same energy across a wider band past one critical bandwidth, and it sounds louder.
Studio myth: RMS amplitude is just the average of a waveform. Actually it's a squared-then-rooted measure, not a plain average - why it tracks loudness better.
All bass pickups are humbucking and hum-free? Not quite — a Jazz Bass uses two single coils that only cancel hum together; solo one and the buzz returns.
Widely believed: being noise-sensitive means having sharper hearing. Really, it's a personality trait about reactivity to noise, not a hearing-acuity measure.
Myth: a cardioid mic hears nothing off-axis. Actually it's typically only 6 dB down at 90 degrees; real rejection sits at 180 degrees, straight behind.
Myth: attenuating a device's output fixes distortion caused by an overloaded input. The clipping already happened upstream -- output attenuation can't undo it.
Myth: colored or heavy vinyl guarantees virgin, premium material. Actually neither proves it, and clean regrind can sound just as quiet.
Myth: moving a VCA master changes a summed audio bus. A VCA has no audio path -- it trims each assigned channel's own gain by the same amount, in decibels.
Myth: a feedback suppressor removes the need for gain margin. Actually it typically buys only a few extra decibels, not a substitute for margin.
Studio myth: a signal reading legal on a peak meter is automatically fine on air. Loudness (LKFS) and peak level are different things -- both must be checked.
Myth: a condenser capsule can drive a cable or input directly. Actually its tiny capacitance needs a high-impedance buffer stage right behind it to work at all.
Myth: every audio waveform is symmetric about zero. Actually asymmetric waveforms are common, and that asymmetry is a real shape, not just a DC offset.
The myth: 192 kHz always sounds better than standard rates. Actually the audible benefit is often marginal while file size balloons, with little to show for it.
Studio myth: fluctuation strength and roughness describe the same wobble. Actually fluctuation strength peaks near 4 Hz modulation, roughness near 70 Hz.
Myth: better electronics can push a mic's self-noise below any floor. Actually thermal motion of air molecules sets an ultimate noise floor no circuit beats.
Common belief: 'presence' and 'air' are the same boost. Actually presence sits around 2-6 kHz for clarity, while air is a higher shimmer above 10 kHz.
Myth: spreading a sound's energy wider always raises loudness. Actually within one critical band it barely matters; only crossing several bands raises it.
Quantization step size is a time interval, like the gap between samples? Not quite — it's an amplitude interval, the size of one bit's worth of level.
Pushing every element loud makes a mix feel bigger? Not quite — that flattens the balance and buries the lead; a mix needs a clear loudness pecking order.
Myth: calibrating monitor level is the same as setting the mix-bus level. Actually calibration sets acoustic SPL at the listening position, apart from the mix.
Myth: a wide theatrical mix can ship as-is for streaming. Actually dialogue gets buried and peaks trip loudness limits - home mixes need a reduced range.
The myth: the Thomson (Bessel) filter has a sharp cutoff like other designs. It trades a gentler roll-off for flat, waveform-preserving group delay.
Common belief: lighter moving mass is always better for a speaker driver. Actually too light a cone can sacrifice strength or bass extension; it's a trade-off.
It's tempting to think dB(A) and dB(C) share one scale. In fact different filters shape them — A cuts far more low end, so the numbers aren't comparable.
Myth: loudness from both ears should simply add, doubling a sound's loudness. Actually the ears partly inhibit each other, giving only ~1.5 times the boost.
Common belief: a vibrating plate rings with evenly spaced harmonic overtones, like a string. Actually its bending-stiffness-driven modes are inharmonic instead.
The myth: feedback is purely a volume problem, so turning down solves it. Actually placement sets the phase conditions that decide what runs away.
Myth: low-noise tape is an electronic noise-reduction system. Actually it's a tape formulation with finer particles — a different fix for hiss entirely.
Myth: a file's extension tells you its codec, like assuming every WAV is uncompressed PCM. Actually the container just wraps the audio - the codec can vary.
The myth: average amplitude and RMS are the same measure. Actually RMS (0.707 of peak for a sine) runs higher than the mean rectified average (0.637).
Myth: an analog delay's repeats should sound as pristine as a digital one. BBD circuits lose highs with each repeat -- that fade is the format's signature.
Myth: neural dyssynchrony is just another form of hearing threshold loss. Actually thresholds can look normal - the real deficit is smeared nerve timing.
Myth: a room has one single resonance pattern to treat. Actually every mode has its own distinct pattern, and the real response sums many of them together.
Myth: parallel compression is just a lower ratio on one insert. Actually it blends a fully dry signal under a heavily squashed copy, keeping real transients.
The myth: noise shaping reduces total quantization noise. Actually it redistributes noise to bands your ears barely notice; total energy rises.
Studio myth: a fader at unity (0 dB) means that channel is off. Unity just means no gain change -- the signal underneath is still passing through unaltered.
The myth: a concert hall's excess reverb can be fixed with EQ. Actually that's architectural — fixed with acoustic design or absorption, not equalization.
Popular belief: nominal operating level is as loud as a device gets. Nominal is the average working point; maximum is the clipping ceiling above it.
Common belief: a louder master always wins. Streaming and broadcast now normalize loudness, so that extra-loud edge gets turned right back down.
Widely believed: a line feed sounds the same as a mic picking up the source acoustically. Really, mic pickup also captures the room around it.
The myth: a diatonic harmonica can play any note in tune. Actually it's built for one major scale; full chromatic notes need bends and overblows.
The myth: you can insert a compressor across a fader group to process it. Actually a fader group carries no summed audio — there's nothing to insert on.
Common belief: a higher sample rate fixes latency. Actually buffer size is the real lever — bigger buffers cut dropouts but add delay between in and out.
Popular belief: A/C/Z weighting and Fast/Slow/Impulse are the same setting. They're different axes -- frequency shape versus how fast the meter reacts.
The myth: any foam on a wall absorbs sound. Actually closed-cell foam's sealed bubbles block airflow, making it a poor absorber despite the acoustic-foam look.
Myth: an amplifier's offset trim is just another gain or bias control. Actually it nulls a static DC error at the output, unrelated to signal gain.
Myth: a horn adds power to a speaker. Actually it adds no power at all; it improves impedance matching and efficiency, like a megaphone, not an amplifier.
The myth: a maximally flat magnitude filter also has flat phase. Actually a Butterworth's magnitude is ripple-free, but its phase response is far from linear.
The myth: mastering plug-ins can fix a poorly balanced mix. Actually balance problems belong in the mix; mastering tools polish an already-good stereo file.
Myth: a telephone hybrid is just a mixer input. Actually without null adjustment and a mix-minus feed, the caller hears their own voice as echo.
Myth: stereo localization relies only on level differences between speakers. Actually low frequencies localize mainly by timing cues, not loudness.
Myth: normal hearing thresholds guarantee normal performance above them. Actually the two differ — quiet detection can be fine while louder processing isn't.
Myth: a real source radiates flat, unspreading plane waves. Actually real wavefronts curve and lose level with distance - plane waves are only an ideal case.
Myth: sensitivity and efficiency are the same figure. Actually efficiency is % power converted to sound; sensitivity is SPL at a set input.
Myth: any reverb effect must build a long decay tail. Actually early-reflection reverb only generates the first sparse echoes, by design.
The myth: an echo chamber produces distinct repeats like a delay. Actually it builds dense natural reverb from a speaker and mic in a hard room.
Myth: spilling a group onto the faders changes its routing. Actually spill only changes what the fader layout shows - the underlying signal path stays the same.
Any DI box can take a speaker-level signal? Not quite — a passive box not rated for that level gets overdriven; DIs are built for instrument-level sources.
A bucket-brigade chip converts audio to digital? Not quite — it shifts analog charge samples down a chain of capacitors - no digital conversion involved.
Studio myth: integrated LUFS is the same as peak level. Actually it's a gated average loudness over the whole program, not the highest sample.
Myth: a flat analyzer curve guarantees a balanced-sounding mix. Equal-loudness hearing means bass and treble seem weaker at low volume -- trust your ears too.
Common belief: spillover is the same as true bypass. Actually bypass routes the dry signal around the effect; spillover lets an existing tail ring out.
Myth: acoustic-era recording horns amplified sound electrically. They were purely mechanical -- no microphone, no power, just a horn shaking a cutting stylus.
The myth: thermal resistance is the same as electrical resistance. Actually it describes how well coil heat escapes, measured in degrees per watt.
Myth: a fixed-ms predelay stays in sync as tempo changes. Actually only a note-value predelay re-syncs automatically; a fixed one drifts off the beat.
The myth: a speaker's voice-coil DC resistance is its rated impedance. Actually the two numbers differ -- resistance is just one input to that rating.
Myth: tube nonlinearity only ever adds pleasant harmonics. Actually pushed hard, the same soft-clipping curve turns overdrive harsh, not just warm.
An omni mic is equally sensitive from every direction at every frequency? Not quite — its pattern narrows at high frequencies as the body shadows sound.
The myth: subglottal pressure mainly sets vocal pitch. Actually it mainly drives loudness — its effect on pitch is only secondary.
Myth: a channel and a bus are the same thing. Actually a channel carries one source; a bus is where several channels get summed together.
The myth: blending a sample under the snare always makes it bigger. Actually without checking phase, the combined hit can sound thinner.
Myth: that bullet in front of a driver is a dust cap. A phase plug aligns sound paths so highs from different parts of the diaphragm don't cancel.
Myth: all plosive consonants pop a mic the same amount. Actually bilabial sounds like p and b carry the strongest low-frequency burst, popping mics hardest.
Myth: an envelope control voltage is itself an audio signal. Actually it's a control signal — route nothing to it and the VCA it should open just stays shut.
Common belief: a large-diaphragm mic's presence peak is always flattering. Actually the 4-5 kHz boost can be excessive, and distance changes the tone too.
It's tempting to think an approved caller goes straight to air. In fact a screener only queues them — the host decides, and can't stop what's said live.
Popular belief: the outer ear is a passive funnel with no effect on tone. Actually it actively filters sound, boosting around 3-4 kHz with real peaks.
It's tempting to think octave-band levels add up arithmetically. In fact they combine on an energy basis — mixing octave with third-octave data isn't valid.
Myth: the numbers printed on a knob are calibrated units. Actually most markings just show relative position, not an exact measured value.
Myth: a high spectrum-flatness value means a sound is loud. Actually it means the sound is noise-like - flatness measures tonal balance, not level.
Myth: any three-pin XLR cable is automatically balanced. Actually balance needs equal impedances on both legs plus a differential input, not just the connector.
Myth: any aux send behaves the same pre- or post-fader. Actually a pre-fader effects send keeps sounding even after the fader is pulled down.
Myth: a sound's pitch comes from its temporal envelope. Actually pitch mostly comes from the fast fine structure inside; the envelope just shapes loudness.
Myth: an object's trim and a renderer's Trim controls do the same job. Actually object trim offsets one sound's level, while renderer Trim cuts whole groups.
Studio myth: parallel compression lowers the loud peaks. Actually blending in a squashed copy raises the quiet parts — peaks stay untouched.
Myth: a higher sample rate widens dynamic range. Sample rate sets frequency bandwidth -- it's bit depth that sets the gap between loudest and quietest signal.
Myth: a loud master impresses listeners on streaming. Actually the platform turns it down to its target — you traded dynamics for nothing.
Myth: swapping in a silicon diode gives the same clipping tone. Actually germanium turns on near 0.2-0.3 V versus silicon's higher threshold - a different clip.
Common belief: an inline pad fixes any distorted mic signal. Actually it only cuts level before the preamp — it can't fix capsule overload.
The channel fader is what sets a clean recording level? Not quite — that's analog gain's job, applied before conversion; the fader just adjusts monitoring.
Popular belief: a carbon microphone works passively, like a dynamic. It needs an external DC current flowing through its carbon granules to function at all.
Myth: an acoustic heat map's warm colors indicate temperature. Actually 'heat' is only a figure of speech — the colors encode sound level, not warmth.
Myth: reviewing the studio feed is the same as checking what aired. Actually an aircheck captures the true off-air signal, including processor effects.
Myth: all ribbon mics need phantom power disabled to stay safe. Actually only passive ribbons are at risk; active ribbon mics require phantom power to work.
Common belief: converting a 16-bit file up to 24-bit adds quality. Actually it only pads the word with zeros — real detail never increases by padding upward.
Myth: all distortion adds new harmonics. Actually linear distortion only reshapes frequency balance and phase, adding no new tones — EQ fixes it, not a limiter.
Myth: a cool tilt always means better clarity. Actually it's just less low-end energy relative to highs, which can also just mean a thin sound.
The myth: air particles ride along with a sound wave across the room. Actually they just oscillate in place - only the disturbance itself travels, near 340 m/s.
Myth: tracks that read fine rarely add up to bus clipping. Many channels' transient peaks can stack and exceed 0 dBFS even when each track looks safe alone.
Myth: a lit signal LED means the channel's level is correctly set. Actually it only confirms signal is present above a low threshold, not that level is right.
Common belief: 0 dB means no signal is present. Actually it just marks the reference point in a ratio — decibels are always relative.
Myth: refraction and reflection describe the same bending of sound. Actually refraction bends a path via changing air speed, reflection bounces off surfaces.
Myth: belting is trained shouting. It's tuned resonance and breath control carrying a chest-quality sound up high - force alone just damages voices.
Myth: a measurement microphone reads flat no matter what field it's in. A free-field mic reads low at treble once you move it into a diffuse, reverberant space.
Myth: a smaller port is fine as long as it fits the box. Actually shrinking a port raises air velocity, causing chuffing at high output.
Myth: a lower speech-in-noise score means worse hearing. Actually a lower (more negative) SNR threshold actually means better performance in noise.
Common belief: heavier saturation always makes a snare bigger. Actually push it too far and the transient turns fizzy — parallel keeps it clean.
The myth: THD+N and THD measure the same thing. Actually THD+N folds in residual noise too, so it's always the larger of the two numbers.
Commonly assumed: a 'chamber' reverb is purely a digital algorithm - but it meant a physical room with a speaker and mics, recorded for natural decay.
Myth: dynamic control just means compression. Actually it covers any level-dependent processing; limiters, expanders, gates, and dynamic EQ all qualify too.
Myth: a resonant air space only rings at one pitch. Actually it has many natural frequencies, not just a single resonance.
Common belief: a 'desk' and a 'console' are different pieces of gear. Actually they're the same mixing console, just British versus US naming.
Myth: distortion from a compression driver at high volume is the amplifier's fault. Actually it's the compressed air in the throat itself turning nonlinear.
The myth: a digital audio receiver outputs analog sound like a DAC. Actually it decodes the bitstream into PCM data — output stays digital.
Myth: bumps in a speaker's response mean a bad driver. Actually cabinet-edge diffraction, sound scattering off sharp edges, often causes that ripple.
The myth: a drum subgroup and a VCA group do the same job. Actually a subgroup sums real audio; a VCA only links faders without summing signal.
Commonly assumed: a decibel is an absolute level - but dB always expresses a ratio; dynamic range is the dB gap between peak and noise floor.
Myth: LZeq measures loudness like LAeq. Actually Z-weighting applies no loudness shaping — it's just the flat, unweighted energy average.
Widely believed: matching peak levels is enough for a fair A/B comparison. Really, you need matched perceived loudness, confirmed by ear — peaks alone mislead.
Myth: every condenser mic needs 48V phantom power. Actually that's just one way to supply polarization; electrets carry a built-in charge.
Common belief: hyperacusis means your ears are extra sensitive in a good way. Actually normal-level sounds feel intolerably loud, often with normal thresholds.
Myth: recalling a speaker layout also restores the channel mix. Actually it typically reloads only monitor routing and calibration, not mix settings.
Myth: an omnidirectional mic stays omni at every frequency. Actually it narrows and beams at high frequencies, just like other polar patterns.
Myth: a meter's Fast/Slow setting is a frequency weighting like A or C. Actually it's a time weighting - it sets how quickly the reading responds, not tone.
Myth: a reversed-polarity cable sounds wrong on its own. Actually it can sound normal alone; the problem appears only when summed with a correctly wired copy.
Common belief: THD and THD+N measure the same thing. Actually THD+N also folds in noise, so it's typically a higher, less flattering number than THD alone.
Myth: any decking panel works fine as a pit filler. Actually fillers are rated for a specific span and load; the wrong platform can't safely bear weight.
Myth: a short circuit and an open circuit are the same fault. Actually a short is near-zero resistance where nothing should connect; an open is a break.
It's tempting to think accurate monitors alone guarantee an accurate mix. Room modes, reflections, and placement usually dominate what you actually hear.
Myth: spectral crest factor is just the usual peak-to-RMS crest factor. Actually that one is time-domain - this compares a spectrum's peak to its average.
Studio myth: every wind instrument overblows to the octave above. Actually the clarinet, with its closed cylindrical bore, overblows a twelfth instead.
Popular belief: a shell hit is basically a rimshot. Actually a rimshot strikes head and rim together; a shell hit hits only the shell for a dry, woody click.
Myth: every ribbon mic needs phantom power. Actually only active ribbons do; passive ribbons generally don't, and phantom can damage them if hot-patched.
Myth: a centered pan plays at the same level as hard left or right. Actually pan law attenuates the center a few dB to keep loudness constant across the sweep.
Common belief: any drum pad can trigger a separate rim-shot sound. Actually only dual- or three-zone pads carry a working rim trigger.
Myth: white noise and pink noise are interchangeable test hiss. Actually white is flat per hertz and sounds bright; pink falls per octave to match how we hear.
A mouthpiece pop is always a mistake to edit out? Not quite — players also use it deliberately as an effect; gating it can cut the real note's attack too.
Common belief: redlining a channel is only a problem once the master bus clips too. On digital gear, that channel itself already risks hard clipping at 0 dBFS.
Myth: an all-pass filter is inaudible since its amplitude response is flat. Actually its frequency-dependent phase shift and group delay can still be heard.
Myth: an LDR responds to light instantly like a photodiode. It's a slow device with lag and memory - and it's a resistor, not an active semiconductor.
Myth: a bubble curtain blocks underwater noise equally at every frequency. Actually low-frequency energy from pile driving passes through it far more easily.
Myth: turning up headphone volume also raises the level being recorded. Actually it only changes what you hear; the recorded signal stays exactly the same.
Does any phase difference between two signals cause cancellation? Not quite - it needs equal level and exactly 180 degrees of offset.
Common belief: DC offset is just a low-frequency thump or idle noise. Actually it's a constant voltage under the signal that eats headroom.
Popular belief: bolting a ground wire to any metal point on the chassis is enough. Actually paint and rust create resistance, causing noise and even fire risk.
Studio myth: the 'loudness' button on a receiver is the same as loudness normalization in streaming. It's a fixed bass boost meant only for quiet listening.
Studio myth: boosting the low-mid band fixes a muddy channel. Actually excess energy is often the problem — cutting the LMF solves it more cleanly.
Myth: a flat end-to-end response means no processing happened. Pre-emphasis boosts highs first; de-emphasis cuts them back after, pushing channel hiss down too.
A MOSFET's gate needs continuous current to stay switched on? Not quite — it's voltage-controlled; the gate draws almost no current once switched.
Myth: any dummy load works for silent amp recording. A resistive load sounds duller -- a reactive load box varies impedance with frequency like a real speaker.
Myth: switching to a quieter microphone lowers the room's actual noise floor. Actually the noise floor belongs to the space, not the mic's electronics.
Common belief: a DJ 'bend' is the same as moving the pitch fader. Actually a bend is a momentary nudge to fix timing, not a lasting tempo change.
Myth: analog wireless transmits audio untouched, like a wire. Actually companding squeezes and re-expands the signal, which can breathe if levels are wrong.
Widely believed: hitting a cajón's center with fingertips gets the deepest bass. Really, a flat-palm strike drives the tone — fingertips thin it and add slap.
Common belief: more low-frequency level always helps speech clarity. Actually within STI, a heavy bass band raises masking and can drag intelligibility down.
Myth: turning down a console's monitor path lowers what's being recorded. Actually the monitor path only affects what you hear; the recorded level is untouched.
Myth: mixing quiet reveals the true tonal balance. Actually bass and treble sound weaker at low levels, per equal-loudness curves - balance shifts with volume.
The myth: a return track and the master track do the same job. Actually the master is where every track sums to a final output; a return is just an aux send.
The myth: more DI in a mic blend always adds clarity. Actually too much DI can sound sterile, and unchecked phase can cancel instead of fill out.
Myth: a higher leakage quality factor QL means a leakier, worse box. Actually higher QL means lower loss - a well-sealed box has the higher number.
Myth: if the meter isn't pinned, nothing clipped. Actually brief peaks can clip and add harsh distortion without ever pinning a meter that averages or lags.
Myth: a speaker's power-handling rating tells you how loud it plays. Actually it's a durability rating — how much power it survives, not a loudness spec.
Myth: sealing a driver in a box lowers its resonance. Actually the trapped air acts as an extra spring, raising resonance above the free-air value.
Myth: planar-magnetic and electrostatic headphones use the same tech. Actually electrostatics need a high-voltage supply; planars use magnets.
Myth: console emulation changes level and routing like a real desk. It mainly adds the desk's tonal color and harmonics - push it hard and subtle turns ugly.
Myth: parallel limiting means limiting the whole signal harder. Actually only a copy gets crushed - blended under the dry path, original peaks stay intact.
The myth: an instrument's formants shift along with the note being played. Actually formants are fixed resonances set by the body or bore, regardless of pitch.
Myth: heavy processing that reads louder always means better on-air loudness. Overdriving it crushes dynamics and can push measured loudness past legal targets.
Myth: a volume knob's position tells you the actual output loudness. Actually loudness also depends on how strong the incoming signal already is.
The myth: a VCA group and a summing bus do the same job. Actually a bus actually mixes signals together; a VCA only ganges levels without summing audio.
Myth: digital automatically sounds better than analog. Actually each medium has its own trade-offs - digital's real edge is editing without generation loss.
Popular belief: DVD-Audio discs play in any DVD-Video player. Actually it's a separate hi-res music format that consumer players rarely supported widely.
Declip tools sound like magic restoration. Actually they estimate the flattened peaks and lower level to fit them in -- lost detail can't fully return.
Myth: a channel fader at 0 dB means the level is correct. A fader only sets gain at the mix stage -- the real level is set upstream by input gain.
Myth: the acoustic horizon is a fixed distance around a listener. Actually it shrinks and grows with background noise and weather.
Myth: a 'constant-voltage amplifier' is the same as a 70V PA distribution system. Actually those are separate systems sharing one name.
Myth: a bloom reverb sounds dense from the very first instant. Actually its character is the gradual swell after onset; fast material may not trigger it.
It's tempting to think crosstalk and separation are unrelated. In fact they're the same measurement — crosstalk is negative dB, separation its magnitude.
Myth: an EQ bell curve boosts only its exact center frequency. Actually it lifts a whole band around that center, tapering off gradually to each side.
Myth: a cabasa is just a gourd shaker, same as an afoxe. Actually the modern cabasa uses a steel ball-chain over a ridged cylinder, a different build entirely.
The myth: more elements in a beamforming array always give a tighter beam. Actually beam width is set by the array's total length, not element count.
Popular belief: cart cues auto-continue like a cue list. Actually each cart button fires manually and independently; there's no auto-follow between them.
It's tempting to think cardioid subwoofer mode boosts front output. In fact it mainly cancels rear radiation, and total level can even drop.
Common belief: same sample rate means two devices are frame-aligned. Actually without a shared clock their frame edges still drift apart.
Myth: sheer loudness equals impact. Actually heavy limiting can make a drop louder while killing its punch — contrast before it matters more.
Popular belief: a wet hire is just gear rental with better service. Actually 'wet' means an operator comes with it; a dry hire is equipment only, no crew.
Studio myth: any studio condenser can serve as a measurement mic. Actually a precision mic meets defined standards an ordinary condenser doesn't.
Myth: adjusting your monitor level changes what actually gets recorded. Actually the record output is a separate feed entirely.
Myth: a loud, steady tone fades the way a soft one does. Actually adaptation is strongest for faint, high tones near threshold; loud or bass tones barely fade.
Common belief: monitor-cue effects also get saved for the mix engineer later. Actually monitor-only effects are never committed to the recorded track.
Myth: 32-bit float gives 32 bits of precision. Actually the significand holds about 24 — and float headroom won't stop a clipped final output.
Myth: Linkwitz-Riley and Butterworth crossovers act alike at crossover. Actually Butterworth is down 3 dB and out of phase there; LR is down 6 dB and in phase.
Myth: coloration always means a flaw to fix. Actually it's the tonal flavor a mic, room, or piece of gear adds - sometimes exactly what you want.
The myth: a production spec and a production plan are the same document. Actually the spec sets required targets to hit; the plan is how you get there.
The myth: thicker plywood absorbs more bass as a panel absorber. Actually added mass and stiffness lower and narrow the tuned frequency instead.
Myth: a reverb swell is just fading up the dry source. Actually it's the wet reverb level itself rising, blooming ambience over time.
The myth: a masked sound gets deleted by the louder one. Actually it's still there, just pushed below the raised hearing threshold nearby.
The myth: latency compensation removes the delay you hear while monitoring. Actually it only shifts the recorded file back into place after the take.
Myth: calibrating a mic always needs a known reference mic. Reciprocity calibration doesn't - a reciprocal mic can play sound as well as capture it.
Myth: T-power is just old phantom power. It puts 12 V across the signal pair, not 48 V on the shield - plug the wrong mic in and you risk damage.
Myth: tire cavity noise is airborne, so more cabin absorption fixes it. Actually it travels structurally through the suspension; absorption barely touches it.
Myth: 'THD' always means the same percentage everywhere. Actually THD referenced to the fundamental and THD referenced to the total give different numbers.
Myth: a more sensitive microphone is a better-quality microphone. Actually sensitivity just means more output per pascal, not lower noise.
Popular belief: a sidestick and a rimshot are the same technique. Actually a rimshot hits head and rim together loudly; a sidestick is a soft, dry click.
Myth: an organ stop's foot number tells you its volume. Actually the foot length marks pitch, not loudness - 8' is unison, 16' is an octave lower.
Myth: passband ripple is always a design flaw. Actually some filters trade ripple for a steeper roll-off; Butterworth just chooses zero ripple instead.
Widely believed: matching tempo is enough to blend two tracks well. Really, mismatched keys still clash — harmonic mixing pairs compatible keys, not just BPM.
Myth: a re-amp box works like a DI box. Actually they convert signal in opposite directions - DI goes instrument-to-line, re-amp goes line-to-instrument.
Myth: a mix that sounds loud is ready for mastering. Ready means adequate headroom, no clipping -- a bus limiter crushing the peaks leaves nothing to work with.
Myth: a node in a standing wave is where the energy died. Pressure nodes are velocity peaks a quarter-wave away - the energy is stored, not gone.
Common belief: a bigger sealed box just adds more bass output. Actually it also lowers the system's resonance and Q by acting as a softer air spring.
Myth: a steady sound fading during exposure means hearing damage. Actually that's normal, reversible auditory adaptation, not a lasting shift.
Myth: early acoustic recordings used microphones. Actually the pre-electric era captured sound purely mechanically, via a horn driving a cutting stylus.
Studio myth: an audience mic just catches general room sound. Actually aim it at the PA instead of the crowd and you capture bleed, not ambience.
Myth: making a vocal sit forward just means pushing the fader up. Actually presence EQ and controlled dynamics do the work - too much reverb pushes it back.
Myth: automatic level control is basically a musical compressor. Actually it forces near-constant output, which can pump audibly on music.
Myth: white noise looks flat on a standard octave-band analyzer. Actually white noise rises 3 dB per octave there; pink noise is the one that reads flat.
Myth: any boundary mic works the same on a small tabletop. The pressure-zone effect needs a surface large relative to the wavelengths involved to work right.
Studio myth: a saxophone's bell radiates its whole sound. Actually much of the tone comes from the open tone holes along the body, not just the bell.
Myth: flatting a channel means muting or turning it down. Actually a flat channel still passes full signal; only its EQ and dynamics get reset to neutral.
The myth: any pole placement works for a digital filter. Actually poles on or outside the z-plane's unit circle make an IIR filter unstable.
Any attenuator pad matches impedance at both ends? Not quite — only a true T-pad or H-pad does that; a simple L-pad does not.
The myth: a flat flexible panel delivers bass and imaging like a cone speaker in a box. Actually thin panels trade low end and imaging for diffuse coverage.
Myth: a Bessel crossover rolls off more steeply than others. Actually it's more gradual — Bessel trades roll-off steepness for accurate, linear-phase timing.
Myth: a thin decorative panel absorbs bass or blocks sound between rooms. Actually PET felt mainly absorbs mid and high frequencies.
Myth: a DCA sums drum channels onto a shared bus like a subgroup. Actually a DCA only scales levels — the audio stays on separate paths.
Common belief: weak-sounding bass needs a low-shelf boost. Actually it's usually mud elsewhere masking the low end, so cutting the offending band helps more.
Studio myth: AFL and PFL are interchangeable ways to solo. Actually PFL solos pre-fader for setting gain, while AFL taps post-fader for its real mix level.
Myth: an HF far setting fixes all high-frequency air loss. Actually absorption also shifts with temperature and humidity - a fixed boost can't cover that.
The myth: fast attack and high ratio do the same job on a compressor. Actually attack sets reaction speed, ratio sets how hard it squeezes.
The myth: a plenum is just empty space above a ceiling. Actually it's part of the air-distribution system, and needs plenum-rated cable when carrying airflow.
Common belief: the kick 'batter head' is the front head facing the audience. Actually it's the back head the pedal's beater actually strikes.
Myth: a bottom snare mic sums fine at its natural polarity. Actually top and bottom heads move oppositely, so non-inverted usually cancels.
Widely believed: plug-in power and 48V phantom power are interchangeable. Really, it's a lower voltage for small electret mics — condensers won't run on it.
Myth: a summing amplifier's inputs interact with and load each other. Actually the virtual-ground node keeps each input's current independent.
Common belief: ducking a reverb return means keying the compressor off the wet signal. Actually it must be keyed from the dry source to open fully.
The myth: a very short sound and a longer one at the same level sound equally loud. Loudness builds with duration only up to about 100-200 ms, then plateaus.
It's tempting to think a shelving EQ keeps rolling off like a filter. In fact it boosts or cuts a set amount, then holds flat like a shelf.
Commonly assumed: small sync slips in Foley go unnoticed — but audiences readily notice footsteps that land off the frame; sync is the whole point.
Myth: a sensitivity switch works as a live volume control. Actually it matches input voltage to full output, not a performance knob.
Studio myth: a vibrating string makes most of an instrument's sound. Actually the string alone moves little air - the soundboard radiates most of the loudness.
Widely believed: quieting sensitivity is just plain sensitivity. Really, it's tied to a stated noise-reduction level, so mismatched figures aren't comparable.
Widely believed: a reed's cane sets an instrument's pitch. Really, tube length and open tone holes set pitch - the reed just drives the vibration.
Commonly assumed: post-roll records new audio after a punch — but it's just playback for context, letting you hear how the section transitions out.
Myth: a QRD diffuser absorbs sound like a foam panel. Actually it mainly redirects energy into many directions, with only minor absorption.
Myth: a playout room is where a show gets produced live. Actually it transmits pre-finished, scheduled content that operators still monitor.
The myth: muting a channel only stops the direct sound. Actually it also kills its post-fader send, abruptly cutting a reverb tail that was meant to ring out.
Myth: a maximizer guarantees a true-peak-safe master. Actually without true-peak metering it can still let inter-sample peaks past the loudness ceiling.
Common belief: a metering plugin shapes the sound it measures. It only displays level and loudness - insert it anywhere and the audio passes untouched.
Myth: floating-point audio can never clip. Actually its internal math has huge headroom, but converters and integer outputs downstream still can clip.
The myth: the setting you prefer in an A/B test is genuinely better. Actually it may just be louder; listeners rate louder options higher unless levels match.
Commonly assumed: breathy voice just means talking quietly — but the vocal folds don't fully close, adding a turbulent, airy noise at any volume.
A hot spot means the whole system's too loud? Not quite — it's a local overlap that needs the offending speaker re-aimed, not a global level cut.
The myth: the touch-and-fader control surface is what processes audio on a digital console. Actually a separate DSP engine does the mixing.
Myth: smoothly interpolating a filter's coefficients always keeps it stable. Actually for recursive (IIR) filters, intermediate values can ring or go unstable.
Commonly assumed: any small vocal booth is ready for ADR — but it also needs a synced picture feed and cueing system, not just isolation.
Myth: a filter's response plot is just its boost-and-cut curve. Actually every magnitude change on that plot comes with a phase shift too, often unshown.
The myth: 'ambient' and 'ambiance' mean the same thing. Actually ambient is the surrounding conditions themselves; ambiance is a room's felt atmosphere.
Myth: boosting presence adds clarity to harsh dialogue. Actually if consonants are already brittle, more presence just worsens it.
Common belief: sound power level is basically sound pressure level. Actually power describes the source itself, independent of distance or room.
Myth: pulling the fader down fixes preamp clipping. Actually distortion added at the preamp stage is baked into the signal - lowering the fader can't undo it.
Popular belief: sends on fader is a separate routing mode from an aux send. Actually it just flips faders to control one bus's send levels.
Myth: any player handles consecutive tracks gapless by default. Actually many lossy formats insert silence at track edges that must be trimmed back out.
A mixing theater is just a fancy music studio control room? Not quite — it's built and calibrated to represent a cinema, sized for film and TV re-recording.
Myth: mixing in 64-bit float improves an already-recorded 24-bit file's resolution. Internal precision protects the math -- it can't add detail never captured.
Studio myth: MCL is one precise number. It's a comfortable range that varies within and between listeners, and it isn't the same as UCL, the discomfort ceiling.
Myth: mixing louder reveals more detail in a track. Actually it mainly biases your ears toward more bass and highs, at the cost of ear fatigue over time.
Myth: decay and release are the same knob. Decay is the fall right after the attack peak; release is the fade after you let the note go.
Myth: a thick, isolated wall can't be compromised by one contact point. Actually a single rigid bridge can carry vibration straight through.
The myth: 'wet' means unprocessed and 'dry' means with effects. Actually it's reversed — wet carries added effects, dry is untouched.
The myth: digital summing sounds worse than an analog bus. Actually with equal gain structure the difference is negligible; phase issues matter more.
Myth: velocity sensitivity and aftertouch are the same thing. Actually sensitivity captures strike force; aftertouch measures pressure after the key is down.
Myth: a speaker flat on-axis sounds flat everywhere in the room. Actually off-axis response can differ a lot, and that's mostly what a room hears.
Myth: Qes is a driver's total damping at resonance. Actually it's only the electrical part, from the voice coil and magnet — total damping also needs Qms.
Common belief: a guitar's phase switch changes tone no matter the pickup selected. Actually it only matters with two or more pickups combined.
Popular belief: a pre-fader send follows the fader down, killing the cue mix too. Actually it stays constant no matter where the fader sits.
The myth: hitting 0 dBFS on a digital peak meter is the target. Actually that leaves no headroom, and a fast peak meter doesn't show loudness like VU or RMS.
The myth: polarity and phase are the same thing. Actually polarity is a sign flip; phase is a time shift, and confusing them misdiagnoses problems.
Myth: insert mix at 100 percent differs from a normal serial insert. Actually they're identical — insert mix just adds the option to blend in dry signal.
The myth: a peak-level reading tells you how loud a track sounds. Actually peak marks the highest point reached; perceived loudness tracks average energy.
Commonly assumed: a passive DI needs phantom power to work - but it's transformer-based and runs on no power at all.
Myth: normalizing to the loudest peak makes two programs sound equally loud. Actually loudness normalization targets LUFS, which matches perceived volume.
Myth: oxygen-free copper conducts dramatically better than ordinary copper. Actually the difference is a fraction of a percent; OFC mainly resists cracking.
Popular belief: a P-channel MOSFET turns on with a positive gate voltage, like its N-channel cousin. Actually it needs the gate driven negative to the source.
Common belief: a foam windscreen doesn't affect the sound at all. Actually it does trim highs slightly, though a correctly sized one costs very little clarity.
Myth: reverb and delay are basically the same effect. Actually reverb builds a decaying wash of reflections, while delay creates distinct, separate repeats.
Popular belief: room reflections can be fixed with EQ afterward. Actually they're a time-domain comb-filter problem; only moving the mic or source fixes it.
Shimmer is only a reverb effect? Not quite — it's also a natural trait, the bright glistening sustain heard in real cymbal decay.
Myth: a mic's negative dBV sensitivity number signals a defect. Actually it's just a lower output level than a less-negative figure - not a fault at all.
The myth: on-ear headphones seal and isolate like around-ear ones. Actually their pads rest on the outer ear with only a partial seal, leaking sound.
Myth: a guitar's direct output already sounds like a miked cabinet. Actually raw DI signal is flat and harsh until speaker emulation adds that coloration.
Popular belief: a VCA master mixes audio together like a subgroup. Actually no audio passes through it; it just remotely trims each channel's own gain.
The myth: a drum trigger can respond with zero latency. Actually scanning the strike to read velocity, plus processing, always adds some delay, however small.
Common belief: limiting and compression are the same tool. A limiter caps peaks hard at a ceiling; compression works more gently across a wider range.
Myth: tilting a compressor's sidechain changes the output tone. Actually the audio stays untouched; only the detector's sensitivity to highs or lows shifts.
The myth: a split-coil bass pickup is just a single coil. Actually its two reverse-wound halves cancel hum like a humbucker, keeping a punchy tone.
Studio myth: one microphone type suits everything. Dynamic, condenser, and ribbon each suit different sources -- the wrong pick costs you tone or headroom.
The myth: a post-fader send is tapped after panning too. Actually it's taken before pan — moving the pan control never changes a post-fader send's level.
Common belief: a pad switch fixes any distortion on loud sources. Actually if the capsule itself overloads, a pad placed after it won't cure the problem.
The myth: loudness range is dynamic range read off a peak meter. Actually LRA comes from the spread of gated loudness values, not peaks.
Studio myth: a louder master is always a better master. Actually normalization turns it down to match others — you traded dynamics for nothing.
The myth: a slow attack on a mix-bus limiter still catches peaks. Actually a limiter needs a fast attack to stop transients, or they pass right through.
Myth: any relay can reliably switch tiny audio signals. Actually power-relay contacts can fail at low currents - that's why gold-plated signal relays exist.
Myth: a bigger control surface means more mixer channels. Channel and bus counts are fixed by the mix engine that does the processing, not the fader count.
Myth: a mic's specs hold no matter the temperature. Actually sensitivity and self-noise can drift in heat or cold, and condensation adds noise as it warms up.
Commonly assumed: stage-left and stage-right are read from the audience's view - but all stage positions are named from the performer's own point of view.
The myth: filter saturation just makes a sound louder. Actually it adds harmonic distortion and mild compression that changes tone, not just level.
Myth: the ratio alone determines how much gain reduction a compressor applies. Actually threshold sets that; ratio only sets the squeeze once triggered.
Common belief: a faceted panel diffuses sound as evenly as a true Schroeder diffuser. Actually angled flats mainly redirect reflections, not fully scatter them.
Myth: dynamic resonance control is just a fixed EQ notch. Actually it only cuts a peak when it exceeds a threshold, leaving the sound alone otherwise.
Myth: heavy compression only flattens small details. Actually it also crushes macro dynamics — the swing between a quiet verse and loud chorus.
Common belief: an active condenser's tone shifts with preamp impedance loading like a ribbon's does. Actually only passive dynamics and ribbons react.
Common belief: clearing a meter's peak-hold indicator fixes the clipping it showed. Actually it only resets the display; the distortion is already in the audio.
Myth: peak-modulation control and loudness are the same job. Actually they need separate attention; over-clipping for loudness just adds distortion.
Myth: pinned meters mean you're using the full range correctly. Actually the red zone marks the top of headroom, not a target - nothing is left for transients.
Myth: the gain range switch is how you fine-tune input level. Actually it picks a broad band — the continuous knob fine-tunes within it.
Myth: a smeared, blurry tone needs more high-end EQ to fix. Actually smearing usually comes from over-fast attack or heavy limiting, not missing treble.
Myth: Max SPL and sensitivity are the same spec. Actually sensitivity is output for a given input; Max SPL is the loudest level before distortion.
Myth: headroom means turning everything up until it's loud. Actually it's the reserve margin below clipping that lets peaks pass clean.
Myth: a directivity spectrogram is a time-based audio display. Actually it plots angle against frequency, showing how a speaker's coverage narrows off-axis.
Common belief: a mic that's fine at room temperature behaves the same in heat or cold. Actually sensitivity and noise can shift under stress.
Myth: digital clipping sounds gentle like analog overload. Actually it's abrupt and harsh, since full scale is a hard ceiling rather than a gradual limit.
Myth: the loudest limiter style is always the best choice. Aggressive modes can pump and distort delicate material -- match style to source.
A horizontal polar map tells you a speaker's vertical coverage too? Not quite — it only shows side-to-side behavior; vertical dispersion is a separate plot.
Myth: measuring an impulse response needs a literal instantaneous impulse. Actually a sine sweep or balloon pop stands in for that impossible ideal.
Popular belief: the amplitude envelope shows a sound's frequency content. Actually it traces only level over time — the outline of loudness, not pitch or tone.
Myth: EQ can fix the hot spots and echoes under a domed ceiling. The curved surface focuses sound geometrically -- treat the shape, not the tone.
Myth: air- and bone-conduction hearing tests measure the same thing. Actually air conduction tests the whole ear; bone conduction isolates the inner ear alone.
Myth: you can EQ out a boundary-cancellation notch. Actually you can't restore energy that's fully cancelled — move the speaker or surface instead.
Myth: acoustic overload point describes a mic's self-noise. Actually it's the opposite — the loudest SPL it can take before distorting.
Common belief: an eyeglass mic stays a constant distance from the mouth. Actually head turns and slipping glasses shift that distance and the level.
Myth: coarse gain control is the same as a fader. Actually it sets the preamp's input sensitivity in big steps; a fine control refines it from there.
Common belief: a neutral, uncolored sound is boring. Actually neutral just means nothing added or subtracted from the recording — uncolored, not lifeless.
Commonly assumed: full-track means stereo — but it's one channel spread across the whole tape width for top signal-to-noise, playing one way only.
The myth: two drivers with the same model number are automatically sensitivity-matched. Actually normal production tolerances can span several tenths of a dB.
Myth: kHz and Hz are casually interchangeable. The k is a factor of 1,000 - read 5 kHz as 5 Hz and you're three orders of magnitude off.
Widely believed: plate reverb gives realistic, room-like early reflections. Really, it has no true early-reflection pattern, just a smooth, dense, bright wash.
Myth: a 'live' broadcast means zero delay to air. Actually stations often add a short broadcast delay on purpose, even though it's called live.
Myth: a subwavelength resonator absorbs sound broadly. Actually it interacts strongly only near its tuned resonance, not across a wide band.
Myth: dBu and dBV use the same voltage reference. Actually dBu is referenced to 0.775V, while dBV is referenced to 1V, different scales entirely.
Myth: doubling a part automatically thickens it. Actually a sloppy, poorly timed double smears the sound instead of adding body.
Myth: a rumble or whine in a turntable or fan is electrical. Worn bearings grind mechanically - and ignored long enough, they seize the motor.
Myth: turning every gain control up near maximum gets the most out of a system. Wrong-stage gain distribution just adds noise or clips early instead.
Myth: an enclosure resonance test is checking the driver's own resonance. Actually it's hunting for the cabinet itself buzzing or ringing, a separate problem.
It's tempting to think a compressor with heavy makeup gain simply 'sounds better.' In fact that's added loudness biasing the judgment, not proof it helped.
Myth: convolving with an impulse response just multiplies samples together. Actually it's a sliding sum of overlapping products, longer than either input.
A compressor or EQ that sounds 'better' actually is better? Not quite — if it's just louder without gain matching, that's loudness bias, not proof it helped.
Myth: a 6 dB level increase doubles how loud something sounds. Actually 6 dB doubles amplitude, not perceived loudness; the two scales aren't the same thing.
Studio myth: an out-of-phase pickup mix just sounds thin. Actually the cancellation always lowers output level too, not just tone.
A leveler and a compressor do the same job? Not quite — a leveler rides gain slowly over the long term; a compressor reacts fast to short transients.
Common belief: loudness depends only on level. Actually the ear sums energy over time, so a longer sound at the same level can seem louder, up to about 200ms.
Studio myth: DIN and ORTF stereo miking use the same spacing and angle. Actually DIN spaces cardioids 20 cm apart at 90 degrees; ORTF uses 17 cm at 110 degrees.
The myth: every drum hit at one velocity is fine since a sampler evens loudness. Actually identical velocities skip layering entirely.
Myth: expanders only ever act on signal below the threshold. Actually upward expansion raises level above threshold, making loud passages louder to add punch.
Common belief: a pop filter means plosives never need fixing later. Actually pops still get through, so engineers tame that burst afterward too.
The myth: a button microphone means a modern small condenser. Actually the name comes from the noisy carbon-button element, not today's mini condensers.
Commonly assumed: every pickup needs steel strings — but optical pickups sense a string's shadow with light, so any string material works.
Myth: a streaming or CD master doubles as the broadcast master. Actually broadcast delivery needs its own loudness, true-peak, and format conformed to spec.
Myth: a fixed sound-pressure level feels equally loud from any direction. Actually head and ear filtering can make one level sound louder from some angles.
Same as the -10 LU relative gate? Not quite - the -70 LKFS absolute gate is a separate step that removes silence first.
Myth: a wider port has more acoustic mass. Actually a larger cross-sectional area lowers acoustic mass - length and end corrections matter more than width.
The myth: any electric-guitar amp works fine for an acoustic instrument. Actually acoustic amps stay flat and uncolored; a guitar amp adds a boxy tone instead.
Myth: a compressor alone is the best way to keep bass consistent. Actually riding the level by hand smooths loudness without the pumping compression can cause.
Myth: analog gear clips abruptly like digital. Actually analog distortion creeps in gradually, so headroom is set to stay clean while beating the noise floor.
Myth: distortion always comes from the last stage before you hear it. Actually it can come from an earlier overloaded stage, innocent gear downstream.
Myth: soloing a channel always reflects its fader level. Actually PFL solos pre-fader at full signal level, while only AFL reflects the fader.
Widely believed: a high-res file guarantees a genuinely high-res recording. Really, the container's specs say nothing about the source actually captured.
Myth: field calibration is the same as full lab calibration. Actually it's a quick on-site check, not a traceable lab-grade calibration.
It's tempting to think recording tape hotter always improves signal-to-noise. In fact push it too far and you trade that gain for distortion and lost headroom.
Studio myth: a spectral freeze is just looping a short slice of audio. Actually it holds a reconstructed spectrum in place, not a repeated waveform chunk.
The myth: a studio monitor should sound pleasing, like hi-fi. It's built to reveal a mix honestly, flaws included, not flatter it with extra bass or sparkle.
Myth: a tape's MOL also shows its high-frequency headroom. Actually saturation output level (SOL), measured with a high tone, often limits treble first.
Myth: a bigger sealed speaker enclosure is a stiffer spring on the cone. A larger trapped air volume is actually more compliant -- a softer spring, not harder.
Common belief: timbre depends only on a sound's waveform. How that harmonic content evolves over time, especially the attack, shapes tone color just as much.
Myth: a pop filter tames harsh sibilant 's' sounds. Actually it's built to break up plosive air bursts like p and b - sibilance needs different treatment.
Common belief: a ported kick head is basically a headless front with a hole. Actually it still works as a full resonant head — the port only vents part of it.
Myth: an absorber panel works just as well fixed flat to the wall. Spacing it on an air gap reaches higher particle velocity there, extending absorption lower.
Myth: a leveling amplifier catches fast transients like a normal compressor. Actually it's built for slow, smooth, program-dependent gain control.
Myth: a mic's incidence angle only matters at low frequencies. Actually diffraction around the mic body changes high-frequency response the most with angle.
Myth: sample rate and bit rate are the same thing. Actually sample rate sets captured bandwidth; bit rate is data flow - raising one doesn't raise the other.
Myth: studio monitors are just nicer-sounding speakers. Actually they favor flat, accurate response over pleasing bass, the opposite goal of consumer speakers.
Myth: phaser stages work like a flanger's short delay. Actually each stage is an all-pass filter shifting phase, not time; more stages just add more notches.
Common belief: matching two amps' front-panel knob positions matches their gain. Actually knob position doesn't guarantee equal gain — the spec must match.
Myth: distortion on a loud source is always the preamp clipping. The capsule or the mic's own electronics can overload first -- more gain won't fix that.
Widely believed: a lower-sensitivity mic is a worse mic. Really, it just needs more gain — quiet ribbon or dynamic mics simply want a clean, high-gain preamp.
It's tempting to think tape headroom and console headroom are the same margin. In fact tape saturates before most electronics clip, and it shifts by tape type.
The myth: any ear tip isolates sound about the same. Actually a poor seal leaks sound and weakens the bass, which is why a custom mold improves both.
Myth: a slow-integrating meter shows the true peak level. Actually slow meters average over time and can miss brief transient peaks entirely.
The myth: a foam windscreen can remove wind noise after it's recorded. Actually foam only prevents turbulence at the mic - it can't undo captured noise.
Myth: a limiter's threshold and input gain do the same job. Actually gain sets how hard you drive the signal in; the ceiling caps how high it can come out.
Myth: analog summing inherently sounds better than digital. Actually DAWs sum with error below audibility - real differences trace to converters, not math.
Commonly assumed: a mastering compressor is basically a limiter — but a limiter stops peaks outright, while a mastering compressor gently levels the whole mix.
Myth: a digital system has zero latency with no long cable run. Actually conversion, DSP, buffering, and transport each add their own delay.
Myth: turning the blend knob makes a compressor work harder. Actually it only sets the wet/dry mix at the output; the compression itself stays the same.
Studio myth: musette-tuned accordion reeds are simply out of tune. Actually the slight detuning is deliberate - it's what creates that shimmering, wet tone.
Myth: any USB-C cable carries Thunderbolt's full bandwidth. Actually only certified Thunderbolt cables carry the protocol, despite an identical connector.
Common belief: a high maximum SPL alone means a mic has wide dynamic range. Actually it also depends on how low the self-noise floor sits.
Myth: peak meters tell you if two songs feel equally loud. Actually peak level doesn't track perceived loudness; that's what LUFS meters are built for.
Myth: distortion from a speaker means the driver is blown. A clipping amp upstream sounds just as ugly - and is often what blows the driver next.
Myth: monitor sends and effects sends are basically the same aux knob. Actually monitor sends are usually pre-fader, so a mix stays put when the fader moves.
Studio myth: more capacitance means more output voltage in a condenser capsule. Actually with fixed charge, voltage falls as capacitance rises - the opposite.
Myth: MIDI velocity compression is audio dynamic-range compression. Actually it edits performance data directly — no audio signal is involved.
Popular belief: a floating balanced output must use a transformer. Actually modern electronically balanced stages can float both legs without one.
The myth: tremolo and vibrato are the same wobble effect. Actually tremolo pulses volume; vibrato pulses pitch - many vintage amps mislabel one as the other.
The myth: a lav mic is directional, so aim matters like a handheld. Actually most lavs are omnidirectional and pick up sound from all around.
Myth: sones and decibels are the same loudness scale. Actually the sone is built so doubling the number means a perceived doubling of loudness, unlike dB.
It's tempting to think a sound keeps its normal loudness once noise is added. Masking eats a share of it -- what survives is the partial loudness.
Common belief: soloing an effect changes the actual mix. Actually wet solo only affects monitoring — it isolates the return without touching the output.
Myth: turning down a later fader fixes clipping from earlier in the chain. Actually clipping is baked into the waveform - a downstream fader can't undo it.
Myth: SNR and dynamic range mean the same thing. Actually SNR is measured against a nominal level, dynamic range against the maximum.
Myth: a marimba's resonator tube sets the bar's pitch. Actually the bar's length and tuning set the pitch; the tube just reinforces the fundamental.
Myth: Sd is a speaker's full frame diameter. Actually it's the effective radiating area — the cone plus roughly a third to half the surround.
Common belief: gain structure just means the master volume fader. Actually it's the level set at every stage, mic to output, so each keeps headroom.
Myth: a pin rail works like a counterweight system's operating rail. Actually pin rail lines are hand-tied with no counterweight; a loaded line can run away.
The myth: digital wireless systems have zero latency. Actually they typically add a few milliseconds of delay, which can matter mixed with wired sources.
Myth: harmonics appear below a note's fundamental pitch. Actually they're always above it; even-order ones, like the octave-up 2nd, are what give warmth.
The myth: acoustic fabric itself absorbs sound. Actually it's just an acoustically transparent cover — the absorption happens in the material behind it.
Studio myth: boomy bass and low rumble are the same problem. Actually boom is a resonant 60-200 Hz buildup, while rumble is much lower, often mechanical.
Myth: the 'black hole music' from Perseus is audible. Actually it's pressure ripples in gas, translated to a pitch about 57 octaves below human hearing.
Myth: a brickwall limiter and a clipper do the same job. Actually a limiter is a fast, time-based process, while a clipper reshapes the waveform instantly.
Myth: AI mastering fixes problems in a bad mix. Actually it just processes what you feed it; a weak mix stays weak after AI mastering.
Widely believed: an aux output always tracks the main output level. Really, it's independent, and can be pre-fader when you expect post-fader.
Common belief: wavelength depends only on frequency. Actually it's speed of sound divided by frequency, so a change in temperature shifts wavelength too.
Myth: 'airy' and 'bright' describe the same quality. Actually airy is very-high-frequency openness above ~12-15 kHz; bright sits lower, in the presence range.
The myth: good in-ear isolation automatically protects your hearing. Actually a sealed IEM can deliver high in-canal SPL from a small-looking signal.
Myth: a console's VCA group is the same as a Blackmer VCA. Actually VCA groups just link fader levels; a Blackmer VCA is a specific analog gain-cell circuit.
Myth: flipping polarity fixes multi-mic comb filtering. Actually the real cause is a time offset — polarity alone can't fully correct it.
Myth: cleaning up a breath means deleting it. Actually breath shaping keeps it, just contouring the attack and decay with fades.
Myth: a weak recorded signal can be fixed later by pushing the fader. Actually that just amplifies the noise already baked in.
Common belief: binaural hearing means stereo. Stereo is a playback format; binaural hearing is your brain comparing tiny time and level gaps between ears.
A close spot mic and a distant main array naturally line up in time? Not quite — sound's travel speed means the spot mic arrives early, needing added delay.
Myth: digital clipping sounds soft like an overdriven analog stage. It doesn't -- digital has a hard 0 dBFS ceiling and clips abruptly and harshly.
Studio myth: a louder vocal wedge always helps a singer hear better. Actually pushing it too hot invites feedback and can muddy the overall stage sound.
Myth: any clipped drum hit is a recording mistake. Sometimes it's deliberate -- a clipper tames sharp transients on purpose to add loudness.
Myth: recording quietly and boosting the level later is harmless. Actually that boost raises the accumulated noise from every stage right along with the signal.
Common belief: no loudness change on the Bing test just means normal hearing. Actually a negative Bing suggests conductive loss, not a healthy ear.
Myth: a heavy speaker cabinet can't resonate. Actually mass alone doesn't stop panel vibration — bracing and damping do.
Myth: album mode re-levels each song on its own. Actually it applies one shared gain offset, so quiet and loud tracks keep their intended balance.
Popular belief: matching hi-fi gear just means matching amplifier watts to speakers. Actually impedance compatibility and sensitivity matter just as much.
Popular belief: blend only means wet-versus-dry effect level. Actually it names any proportion between two combined signals, including two mics on one source.
The myth: a flat measured response is the goal. Actually a flat in-room response often sounds too bright — good balance is usually gently sloped.
The myth: a pipe's ring frequency is just its lowest natural frequency. Actually many shell modes sit well below it - ring frequency marks a distinct mode.
Myth: a warm-up DJ should drop peak-time anthems early to hype the room. Actually that burns the headliner's best moments and leaves nothing to build toward.
Myth: LAFmax is the same as a true peak reading. Peak has no time constant; LAFmax uses A-weighting plus a 125 ms Fast time constant, so it reads differently.
Common belief: more pixels always means a sharper picture. Actually the extra detail stops being visible past a certain viewing distance.
The myth: a pan pot and a balance control do the same job. Actually a pan pot places a mono source in the field; balance only shifts an existing stereo pair.
Studio myth: flipping a mic's orientation changes its actual polar pattern. Actually it only changes which direction that pattern points.
The myth: magnetoresistive heads sense voltage like inductive ones. Actually they sense resistance change instead, staying sensitive even at slow speeds.
Myth: a microphone that isn't flat must be faulty. Actually a shaped response is often deliberate, boosting or cutting bands on purpose for a specific job.
Myth: a raised-cosine filter kills intersymbol interference at every moment. Actually it only guarantees zero interference at the exact sampling instants.
Myth: throttling a fan back always makes it quieter. Actually pushing it toward stall raises noise even as flow drops; separated airflow is the loud part.
Myth: a mic's pressure sensitivity and free-field sensitivity are the same number. Free-field sensitivity adds the diffraction gain around the mic body.
Myth: any XLR cable will pass phantom power to a condenser mic. Actually that depends on correct wiring, not just having three pins.
Myth: wireless transmitter sensitivity is about RF reception. It's actually the audio input gain -- set too high, it just overmodulates and distorts.
Myth: a wool felt panel absorbs deep bass. Actually its thinness limits it to mid and high frequencies; bass needs a different treatment.
Myth: a compressor's gain computer is what measures signal level. Actually that's the detector's job — the computer decides the reduction.
Myth: a mic with low sensitivity is lower quality. Actually low sensitivity on a high-level mic is deliberate, so it handles loud sources without distorting.
Myth: crosstalk is another name for distortion or noise. Actually it specifically measures leakage from a driven channel into a quiet, undriven one.
Myth: pushing a PA past its limit just adds volume. Actually it drives amps into clipping, and the flat-topped waveform can destroy loudspeakers.
Myth: a maximally flat phase (Bessel) filter cuts off steeply. Actually its priority is flat group delay, traded for a gentler roll-off.
The myth: louder mixes are more dynamic. Heavy loudness processing that raises average level usually shrinks a program's actual dynamic range.
Myth: obstruction and occlusion are the same thing. Actually obstruction blocks only the direct path — reflections still get through; occlusion blocks both.
Myth: a guitar's body amplifies the string's energy. Actually it adds no power; it radiates the string's motion far more efficiently through a larger surface.
Myth: carbon-film resistors match metal-film for low noise and tolerance. Actually they fall short of metal-film - just a step up from carbon composition.
Myth: embouchure is just lip position. Actually the jaw, tongue, and facial muscles shape it too - and forcing pitch by pressing harder just tires the player.
The myth: delay time controls how many echoes repeat. Actually that's feedback; delay time only sets the gap before the first repeat.
Myth: more termination resistors mean a cleaner digital signal. Actually only the line's ends should be terminated; terminating every device loads it down.
Myth: roughness and fluctuation strength are the same sensation. Roughness peaks near 70 Hz of modulation; fluctuation strength peaks much slower, near 4 Hz.
Myth: a higher Qtc in a sealed box means deeper bass extension. Actually it means a peakier resonance, not more extension - it can just sound boomier.
Myth: an aux send feeds the main mix. It feeds only the auxiliary bus - a separate mix for monitors, headphones or effects, independent of the mains.
Myth: a buried instrument just needs its fader pushed up. Actually it's often masked by competing frequencies; cutting those elsewhere usually works better.
Myth: a louder room automatically means a hotter electrical signal. Microphone sensitivity links the two -- pascals and volts are different physical quantities.
Studio myth: bus EQ or compression only shapes the overall blend. Actually it processes every channel routed there together; one move affects the whole group.
Common belief: anechoic means soundproof. The wedges stop reflections inside the room, not sound passing through walls - no echo is not no leakage.
A click or dropout on a wireless mic means a dead battery or bad cable? Not quite — it's often an RF hit, brief radio interference stepping on the signal.
Myth: a brief flash of an overload LED means the signal is clipping continuously. Actually a quick flash on a transient differs from sustained clipping.
Is a sudden dropout on tape a recording error? Not quite - a physical crease in the backing can lift the tape off the head at that exact spot.
Myth: grouping tracks in a stack always changes their routing. Actually only a summing stack routes tracks to a shared bus; a folder stack just groups control.
Myth: a louder tone is automatically more prominent. Prominence depends on how far a tone rises above the noise in its own critical band, not raw level.
Myth: Loudness Range is just another name for dynamic range or crest factor. Actually LRA is a gated statistical measure of loudness variation.
Myth: turning the volume up helps an ear with recruitment hear better. It just pushes sounds toward discomfort faster -- compression helps, not more level.
Popular belief: a GPI trigger carries addressed commands like MIDI. Actually it's just a simple on/off contact closure or voltage edge, no data, just a switch.
Myth: more bits removes quantization noise entirely. Actually it only lowers it, about 6 dB per bit — and without dither it's correlated distortion, not hiss.
Studio myth: a log-mel spectrogram and MFCCs are the same representation. Actually MFCCs apply a further transform on top of the log-mel spectrogram.
Sound waves ripple up and down like water waves? Not quite — sound is longitudinal; air compresses and stretches along the same line it travels.
