Myth: fixed-point DSP can only store whole numbers. Actually it commonly represents fractions too, using formats like Q15, just with careful scaling.
Myth: a bigger horn is always louder, regardless of the driver. Actually loudness depends on how well the horn's throat matches the driver, not size alone.
Myth: sound pressure and ambient air pressure are roughly the same size. Actually sound is a tiny ripple riding on ambient pressure, which is vastly larger.
Myth: background noise only disrupts memory if it's loud. Actually what matters is whether it keeps changing, not how loud - concentrating harder doesn't help.
Myth: an amp's input sensitivity spec tells you its output power. Actually it's the input voltage needed to reach rated power, not a power measure.
Myth: speaking as low as possible is always best. Actually a habitually low pitch is a common cause of vocal strain; optimal pitch is about ease.
Myth: locators and markers are the same thing in a DAW. Actually locators define an active start/end range for looping or export; markers are just flags.
Common belief: aiming a mic off-axis only makes it quieter. Actually it usually dulls or colors the tone too, since off-axis response is rarely flat.
Common belief: every player hears the same mix as the main recording. Actually the headphone cue mix is separate, and each player can get their own balance.
Common belief: PCM audio is compressed like an MP3. Linear PCM, the format behind CDs and DAT, is uncompressed -- every sample is stored directly.
The myth: a peak voltage limiter and an RMS/thermal limiter guard against the same thing. Actually the peak type protects excursion, not voice-coil heat.
Common belief: capping a pipe's open end makes it sound higher. Actually a stopped pipe sounds about an octave lower than an open one that size.
Myth: overdrive and fuzz are the same distortion. Overdrive gently soft-clips for a warm, pushed-amp tone; fuzz and hard distortion clip far more aggressively.
The myth: a top snare mic's exact placement barely matters for tone. Actually too high or aimed at the rim loses crack and picks up cymbal.
The myth: speaker sensitivity is the same as max SPL or power handling. Actually it's just output per watt - mismatched sensitivity unbalances a system.
A passive T-pad can add a bit of gain when you need more level? Not quite — it can only attenuate; it's a fixed, matched-impedance loss network.
Myth: a mic's tonal character all comes from its capsule. Actually the output transformer adds its own coloration too, easily mistaken for capsule tone.
The myth: heavy processing can rescue a poorly recorded podcast voice. Actually no chain fixes a bad capture; clean recording matters more than fixing it after.
The myth: ducking a delay return is just turning its level down. Actually it's dynamic — the echo drops while the source plays, then swells back.
It's tempting to think turning monitors up reveals more detail. In fact it just tires your ears faster and pushes you toward misjudging the mix.
Tape flux level and electrical dBu level are the same scale? Not quite — they're different references entirely; the two readings don't equate.
Myth: a small open-baffle speaker can still produce deep bass. Actually the rear wave cancels the front at low frequencies, cutting bass well before that.
Myth: foldback is the same mix the audience hears out front. Actually it's a separate monitor feed set on the aux sends, independent of the house mix.
Myth: moving closer to a mic only makes you louder. Actually proximity also boosts bass on directional mics and reduces the room sound picked up.
Myth: instrument and line inputs are interchangeable. Actually impedances differ greatly — plugging a guitar into a line input loads the pickup and kills highs.
Studio myth: otoacoustic emissions are echoes of the test sound bouncing back. Actually the cochlea actively generates them itself.
The myth: LUFS and dBFS measure the same thing. Actually dBFS is sample peak; LUFS is K-weighted perceived loudness, two entirely different numbers.
Myth: when a performer asks for 'more everything,' cranking every monitor channel is the fix. Actually clarity often comes from lowering competing sources.
Myth: a VU meter shows true peak levels. Actually its slow ballistics show average level, hiding brief transient peaks entirely.
Common belief: soft saturation is essentially distortion-free. Actually it still adds harmonics, just introduced gradually instead of clipped abruptly.
Myth: fixing a polarity error just needs a bit of delay. Actually delay corrects timing, not a sign flip; a polarity error needs the signal literally inverted.
Myth: rolled-off treble always sounds bad. Actually a gentle high-frequency roll-off can tame harshness — and it may be the room, not the source, doing it.
Myth: a Butterworth filter has ripple like a Chebyshev. Actually it's maximally flat, just a smooth 3 dB-down cutoff and steady roll-off.
Myth: loudness rises step for step with decibels. It's a compressive power curve -- roughly a 10 dB rise is needed just to double perceived loudness.
Common belief: a Bessel filter cuts as sharply as a Butterworth of the same order. Actually its gentle roll-off trades sharpness for cleaner transient timing.
Myth: listening with two ears makes a sound twice as loud. Actually binaural loudness is only about 1.5 times louder than one ear alone.
Popular belief: every quarter-inch jack is balanced TRS. Actually many instrument jacks are two-conductor TS, and TRS may carry unbalanced stereo instead.
The myth: two equal sources always sum to +6 dB. Actually only identical in-phase signals do that; uncorrelated sources add to just +3 dB.
Myth: gain trim set on a quiet soundcheck line covers every take. Actually a later belted line can clip if trim leaves no headroom for it.
Myth: a limiter on the output makes a broadcast compliant. Actually compliance is judged by integrated LUFS/LKFS loudness, not just peak control.
Commonly assumed: a broadcast clipper alone should handle all level control — but it's meant to shave brief peaks past upstream AGC and limiting, nothing more.
Myth: louder always means more impact. Actually impact comes from the contrast between loud and quiet - squash that gap and the punch disappears.
Myth: how far away a source sounds is set by reverb time. It's the direct-to-reverberant balance - more direct reads close, more wash pushes it back.
Popular belief: the singer's formant means singing louder. Actually it comes from reshaping the vocal tract, clustering resonances 3-5, not raw volume.
Myth: a transducer's matching layer should match the crystal's own impedance. Actually it's tuned to the geometric mean of crystal and load impedance instead.
Myth: a spot mic just needs to be loud enough. Undelayed, it arrives ahead of the main pair and comb-filters - align it, and use it sparingly.
Myth: any mic transformer can safely pass 48V phantom power. Actually not every transformer is rated for that DC — the wrong one risks core saturation.
The myth: air molecules fly from a speaker to your ear. They just vibrate in place, handing pressure changes along - the wave travels, the air stays.
Myth: turning up the DAW master fader is how you adjust listening volume. Actually that changes the mix itself; a monitor controller adjusts only what you hear.
Myth: any measurement mic works the same in a reverberant room. Actually diffuse-field mics need random-incidence correction to read correctly there.
Myth: a channel's fader is what sums signals into a mix. Actually the fader just sets level; a dedicated summing amplifier combines the currents into one bus.
Myth: recalling a reference-monitor preset also corrects your room's acoustics. Actually it only standardizes level and tonal settings; the room stays as is.
Studio myth: normalizing a track is the same as compressing it. Normalization applies one constant gain change -- it never touches the signal's dynamics.
The myth: blending a processed copy under the dry track is always safe. A latent or phase-shifting parallel path lands offset and partly cancels the blend.
Common belief: a coverage plot at one frequency tells the whole story. Actually highs narrow more than lows, so one band misses real hot spots.
Myth: boosting a band to hunt for a resonance is harmless prep work. Actually forgetting to flip that boost into a cut leaves the resonance worse, not tamed.
Myth: supercardioid and hypercardioid mics null out straight behind, at 180 degrees. Actually their rear nulls sit near 126 and 110 degrees.
Popular belief: reducing bit depth just means dropping the extra bits. Actually truncating without dither adds harsh, correlated distortion, not benign noise.
Myth: distortion-limited output figures are all measured alike. Actually the rating hinges on a chosen THD threshold, so different thresholds aren't comparable.
Myth: perceived loudness fades exactly as fast as it built up. It actually decays more slowly than it rises, so a sound seems to linger after it stops.
Myth: high-level and line inputs are interchangeable. High-level takes speaker wires from a factory radio - feed it line-level RCA and levels are all wrong.
Myth: fixing a honky voice means cutting a wide swath of midrange. Actually a narrow notch at the exact resonance clears the honk without thinning the tone.
Myth: an electronic drum kit is silent since the sound comes from a module. Actually pad and pedal strikes still make audible mechanical tapping noise on stage.
Common belief: a send and an insert process the whole signal the same way. Actually a send routes a parallel copy to a bus; an insert works in series.
The myth: heavy bus compression added late fixes a mix's glue. Actually deep ratios or a late add cause pumping; it works best set gently and early.
Myth: a C-weighted average can replace a peak reading. Actually LCpeak catches brief impulses an average misses, risking hearing damage.
Myth: sending a channel to both a subgroup and the main mix is harmless. Actually it sums the signal twice, making it louder or phasey.
Myth: mixing an ad hot gets it on air louder. Every spot is measured and normalized to the program's loudness target - that's why ads no longer jump out.
The myth: picking the wrong level on a switchable calibrator is a small error. Actually mixing up 94 dB and 114 dB throws every later reading off by 20 dB.
Myth: you hear your own voice the same way listeners do, entirely through the air. A large part of it reaches you through bone and tissue conduction instead.
Myth: pricier gear always means higher fidelity. Actually fidelity means accurate reproduction of the source, and cost doesn't guarantee that.
Myth: a dead monitor feed means a broken send or cable. Actually check the aux master first; leaving it down silences every channel feeding that bus.
Widely believed: word length controls the highest frequency you can record. Really, bit depth sets dynamic range and noise floor; sample rate governs bandwidth.
Myth: lowering crest factor always makes a mix louder for free. Push it too far and transients flatten -- push it further still and you risk audible distortion.
Myth: a VCA group works like a subgroup bus, summing the channels' audio. Actually a VCA only controls level remotely - the audio is never mixed together.
Myth: a pure tone excites just one point in the cochlea. Actually it spreads across a region, producing a smooth hill on the excitation pattern, not a spike.
Myth: a track gone silent in the mix must be muted. Actually disabling its parent send cuts it from the group just as silently; check that first.
Myth: a condenser is always the best choice of mic. Dynamics handle loud, close sources better, and a condenser's presence peak can turn harsh.
Myth: a directional mic ignores everything off to the sides. Actually it only attenuates off-axis sound, and by how much varies with frequency.
Myth: you should monitor through the DAW while direct monitoring is on. Run both and you hear two offset copies - a flangey double of your own voice.
Myth: rounding and truncation are the same thing. Actually truncation just drops bits and adds a DC bias; rounding picks the nearest value and stays centered.
Myth: on a shared stage box, any console can freely change the analog preamp gain. Actually only the owning console controls it; others apply digital trim.
Studio myth: RC and NC ratings measure room noise the same way. Actually RC (room criterion) judges spectral balance too, not just overall loudness like NC.
Myth: keeping a speaker's limiter LED lit is the goal for maximum loudness. Actually steady illumination means the system is in protection, crushing dynamics.
Myth: a closed, rigid pipe end creates a pressure node. Actually closed ends form pressure antinodes; open ends are where pressure nodes occur.
The myth: auto gain sets the perfect level so you can skip the meter. Actually it's just a starting point - noise or bleed during setup can throw it off.
Common belief: a low-cut filter fully fixes a breath pop. Actually once the capsule's already overloaded by the air blast, EQ can't undo the thud.
Myth: a DSP's output bit depth matches its internal math precision. Actually accumulators run wider, guarding against rounding loss before the final cut.
Commonly assumed: a thin, papery sound means a bad mic or room - but it's usually fast-attack compression or transient enhancement stripping out body.
Myth: tape bias and high-frequency EQ can be set in any order. Actually bias strongly shapes HF response, so it must be dialed in before record EQ.
The myth: a pressure (omni) mic stays non-directional at every frequency. Actually it narrows at high frequencies once wavelength nears diaphragm size.
Commonly assumed: a 12-string needs a chorus pedal for its shimmer — but the octave-paired strings already chorus themselves; a pedal just muddies it.
Myth: a short-term or momentary loudness reading is the delivery spec. Program loudness is the gated integrated average across the whole show, not one instant.
Popular belief: applying dither more than once in a mastering chain adds safety. It doesn't help and can add noise -- apply it once, at the final bit-depth cut.
Common belief: sidechain compression means putting a compressor on the vocal. Actually the vocal triggers reduction on another track entirely.
Myth: a loudspeaker radiates evenly in every direction. Actually only low frequencies spread widely; highs beam narrowly as wavelength shrinks against the cone.
Myth: pitch wobble in a Mellotron is a fault to fix. Actually that drift is inherent to the tape-playback mechanism and is part of the classic sound itself.
Common belief: adding more microphones fixes a tone problem. Actually extra mics usually add phase interference instead of solving the original issue.
Myth: automation removes the need to monitor a broadcast. Wrong-source and stuck-file failures are exactly what automation misses but a listener catches.
The myth: the ear responds equally to all frequencies at a given level. Actually equal-loudness contours show far more level is needed at low and high ends.
Commonly assumed: turning up headphone/cue level changes the main mix everyone hears - but it only adjusts your own headphone feed.
The myth: pressing the keys harder makes an accordion louder. Actually dynamics come almost entirely from bellows movement, the speed and force of the air.
Myth: the audition or cue bus is safe to leave a source patched to. Actually only the program bus goes on air; mixing them up can send a preview live.
Studio myth: a weak tape signal means a worn, degraded reel. Actually some formulations are simply low-output by design, needing more gain and less headroom.
Myth: a thin, hollow sound when combining signals is an EQ problem. Actually it's often a pin-two polarity mismatch; some legacy gear wires pin 3 hot.
The myth: leaving a mic's pad on for quiet sources is harmless. Actually it worsens signal-to-noise and adds hiss; a good pad cuts level only, not tone.
Myth: a mic's lab-stated sensitivity holds true anywhere. Actually it's defined at fixed reference conditions and needs correcting for real-world temperature.
Myth: flipping polarity fixes piano mic phase problems. Actually inversion only reverses sign; it doesn't fix a time or distance offset between mics.
Common belief: 0 dBFS on a sample-peak meter means no clipping. Actually true peaks between samples can exceed 0 dBTP and distort after conversion.
Myth: a ported enclosure helps bass at any frequency below tuning. Actually below tuning the port unloads the cone, letting excursion spike dangerously.
The myth: an RMS detector reacts to every sharp transient. Actually it averages level over time, so brief peaks slip past it - that's a peak detector's job.
Studio myth: boosting treble EQ adds new harmonics to a sound. Actually EQ only lifts overtones that already exist; it can't create harmonics that aren't there.
Myth: two tracks with the same peak dBFS are equally loud. Actually K-weighted LUFS reflects perceived loudness; matched peaks can still sound very different.
Widely believed: a VU meter shows true peak levels. Really, its defined attack and decay ballistics make it read an averaged level, not the peak.
Myth: K-weighting is just old A-weighting renamed. Actually it's a different filter — a head-modeling shelf plus a high-pass, built for loudness metering.
Myth: a mic pad reduces the sound pressure hitting the diaphragm. Actually it only lowers the electrical signal afterward; the capsule sees full pressure.
Common belief: LKFS and LUFS are different loudness units. They're the same measurement under two names -- one from broadcast standards, one from the EBU.
The myth: input trim is for big level changes. It's a fine calibration control -- large adjustments belong on the main gain, not the trim.
Popular belief: combining two noise sources always adds up to a 6 dB rise. Actually uncorrelated noise adds in power, giving only about 3 dB unless correlated.
The myth: a limiter alone can manage dialogue's loudness. Limiting alone just squashes speech -- crest is better tamed with leveling and compression together.
Myth: a peak in a headphone's response always comes from the driver. Actually it can be the ear cup's trapped-air cavity resonating instead.
A mic's sensitivity spec applies no matter the angle? Not quite — it's measured strictly on-axis; off-axis sound gives noticeably less output.
The myth: a mic's pad switch changes its tone. A well-designed pad like -18 dB just lowers level for loud sources -- frequency response stays essentially flat.
Headroom and dynamic range sound interchangeable. They're not -- headroom is the margin above nominal level; dynamic range spans down to the noise floor too.
Commonly assumed: solo (PFL) is automatically level-matched to the mix. On many consoles it isn't -- you must trim it yourself.
Myth: R128 and the US A/85 spec share one loudness target. Europe delivers at -23 LUFS, ATSC A/85 at -24 LKFS - close enough to trip up a delivery.
Myth: ERB is just another name for the Bark critical-band scale. Actually they're similar but distinct, and ERB widens with frequency instead of staying fixed.
Myth: dialnorm metadata is just a label with no effect. Actually a mismatched value makes the decoder attenuate the program wrongly.
The myth: more compression is always fine for a mix. Actually a fast attack can flatten micro dynamics, the tiny detail in a drum's attack.
Common belief: any smooth-looking response counts as flat. Actually flat is judged within a stated tolerance and frequency range - smooth alone isn't enough.
Myth: if a sound system makes noise, it's working correctly. Actually verification checks polarity, wiring and distortion before any tuning.
The myth: rustle noise on a lav means a faulty capsule. Actually it's almost always clothing brushing the mic; remounting fixes it, not swapping the mic.
It's tempting to think 'smooth' means dull. In fact smooth keeps detail while removing harshness; dull loses the highs entirely.
"Linear" or "Flat" on old meters sounds like a fixed standard. It wasn't -- today's standardized flat response is what's now called Z-weighting.
Myth: negative refraction breaks the rule that energy must flow forward. Actually only the phase velocity reverses - energy still moves the normal way.
The myth: any comfortable volume works for mixing. Actually a fixed, calibrated reference level keeps loudness judgments consistent between sessions.
Myth: two voices gently beating against each other means one is simply out of tune. It's often deliberate detuning -- the shimmering 'wet' chorus effect.
Myth: a converter's spec-sheet dynamic range is what you get. Actually real noise, distortion, and gain staging shrink it below that theoretical number.
Myth: a crossover output is always 3 dB down at the crossover point. Actually Linkwitz-Riley outputs are 6 dB down there and stay in phase, summing flat.
Myth: channel level and input gain are the same knob. Actually the fader sets mix contribution downstream of gain, which sets how hot the signal enters.
Myth: miking strings up close like a drum captures a bigger sound. Actually close miking exaggerates bow scratch and one body resonance, not the blend.
Myth: a tape's magnetic sensitivity is set by the user while recording. Actually particle orientation is fixed at manufacture, aligned before the coating dries.
Cranking snare tension to kill buzz sounds like a fix. Actually it can choke the wires against the head and deaden the whole drum instead.
Myth: dulled hearing after a loud show is harmless since it recovers. Actually repeated fatigue before recovery can turn permanent.
Myth: a graphic EQ slider's marked value is exactly what you're getting. Adjacent bands interact, so the real curve shifts from what the sliders show.
Myth: a discrete preamp automatically sounds better than an IC-based one. Discrete just means separate transistors -- a design choice, not a quality guarantee.
Is a silent condenser mic broken? Not quite - it's often just missing or weak phantom power; a tester confirms the voltage before you blame the mic.
Studio myth: old MIDI's current-loop signaling plugs straight into USB or 5V logic. Actually the two signaling schemes aren't compatible without an interface.
Commonly assumed: glued items can always be split apart later - but gluing renders splits and fades into one new file; keep a copy if needed.
Myth: floating-point headroom means a mix can never clip. Actually only internal float stages are protected - the final fixed-point export still clips.
The myth: Slow meter weighting still catches brief peaks accurately. Actually its one-second averaging smooths them away; use Fast or peak mode instead.
Does louder always sound better in a mix? Not quite - preserving crest factor, the gap between peaks and average level, often sounds punchier.
Myth: a picowatt is roughly the same tiny amount as a microwatt or nanowatt. Actually a picowatt is 10^-12 W, orders of magnitude smaller than either.
Myth: a wider guard band is free insurance. Actually every bit of it narrows the usable track and lowers signal-to-noise ratio.
Myth: phons and decibels are the same unit. Actually they only coincide at 1 kHz; equal dB SPL elsewhere doesn't mean equal loudness.
dBZ looks like it must mean the same thing every time you see it. In acoustics it's flat Z-weighting; in radar it's an unrelated reflectivity unit.
Myth: feedback ducking and output ducking do the same job. Feedback ducking limits how many repeats build up; output ducking only lowers their level.
Studio myth: pushing a broadcast processor harder always sounds better. Actually overdoing it causes listener fatigue and audible distortion.
Myth: any quiet, treated room counts as critical-listening. Actually the standard sets specific tolerances for reverb, noise, and speaker geometry too.
Myth: alternate monitor speakers share the mains' volume trim. Each ALT pair typically has its own separate trim, so they need matching by ear or meter.
Myth: momentary LUFS is a good measure of a program's overall loudness. Actually its 0.4-second ungated window swings far more than the integrated value.
Myth: a condenser mic's diaphragm is solid metal. Actually it's thin plastic film with a gold coating only nanometers thick, just enough to conduct.
The myth: the 14 in K-14 is a loudness target. It's headroom - the meter's 0 sits 14 dB below full scale, a Bob Katz reference for dynamic pop and rock.
Myth: a microphone's acoustic port is just a hole and doesn't matter. Blocking or resizing it changes sensitivity, directionality, and frequency response.
Studio myth: a DI signal running through a plug-in chain is still 'dry.' Dry means unprocessed -- any effects chain, even subtle ones, makes it wet.
Myth: heavy multiband processing lets you skip loudness targets. Actually it shapes tone and consistency, but you still must hit the loudness spec.
Studio myth: sound power level and sound pressure level share one reference. Actually sound power level is referenced to one picowatt, a different quantity.
Myth: envelope segments are always straight ramps. Actually a logarithmic envelope curves, matching how we hear loudness - often sounding more natural.
Myth: any level meter shows fast peaks accurately. Actually an averaging VU meter smooths transients away - real peaks need a peak or true-peak meter.
Myth: beats between two close pitches create a new tone. It's an amplitude pulsation as the waves reinforce and cancel, at a rate equal to their frequency gap.
Myth: pulling the master fader down cures a clipping console. If the input gain stage is what's overloaded, the master fader can't reach that clipping at all.
Myth: two signals at the same average level sound equally loud. The ear is less sensitive to low and very high frequencies, so spectral content matters too.
Studio myth: cupping a handheld mic's grille just adds warmth. It ruins the cardioid pattern and is a common cause of feedback onstage.
Myth: a well-designed mic capsule has no resonance at all. Actually every diaphragm has one; good design just places it high and damps it smooth.
Myth: IFB is a two-way intercom between talent and producer. Actually it's one-way — talent listens but can't talk back on that line.
Myth: a single loud SPL reading tells you if noise exposure is unsafe. Actually a dosimeter tracks cumulative dose over time; duration matters as much as level.
Myth: padding a mic then adding back the same gain is harmless. Actually it restores level but raises the noise floor for no real benefit.
Myth: a compressor changes tone like EQ does. Actually it reduces gain above a threshold, shrinking the gap between loud and quiet, not tonal balance.
Myth: an input pad reduces distortion inside a mic's capsule. Actually the pad only protects the electronics that follow, not the capsule itself.
Myth: every mic responds the same regardless of vertical angle. Actually side-address and multi-capsule mics color sound differently above and below axis.
Myth: load and line regulation are the same spec. Load regulation is voltage sag as current demand rises - why weak supplies drop rail voltage on big notes.
The myth: a loud peak means wide dynamic range. Actually peak level and dynamic range are separate — you need loudness-range readings too.
The myth: a saved processing preset is safe to reload for any content. Actually one built for a format or daypart may miss the current target.
Studio myth: false triggers between electronic drum pads mean a broken module. Actually it's usually vibration crosstalk between pads sharing a stand or rack.
Myth: a piezo pickup plugs into any input fine. Into a low-impedance input its bass rolls off and it turns thin and quacky - it wants a buffer or hi-Z DI.
Myth: Nashville tuning is a bright alternate rhythm tuning on its own. Actually it's thin solo; it's meant to layer on top of a standard-tuned guitar.
Myth: a recorder's response is roughly even, so extremes don't need much attention. Actually sweep-revealed errors are usually largest at the extremes.
Popular belief: mics with the same model number are automatically matched. Actually normal manufacturing tolerance still applies, and phase matters too.
It's tempting to think skipping a window leaves a spectrum unweighted. In fact no window still applies one, with high, slow-decaying side lobes.
Myth: any metal contact works for a low-level switching circuit. Dry circuits carry too little voltage to break surface films -- they need gold contacts.
Myth: turning up your monitor level changes the mix you're recording. It only changes what you hear -- the underlying signal never moves.
Studio myth: line-level gear should be impedance-matched, source equal to load. Actually it uses bridging — a high load impedance — for max voltage.
The myth: a stereo mic's output is always ready-to-use left/right. Actually mid-side output needs decoding first, or it stays an undecoded M/S pair.
Studio myth: a sealed sub box hits as hard as a ported one the same size. Actually sealed trades output for tighter, more accurate transient control.
Myth: a sidechain low-pass filter dulls the audio itself. Actually the audio stays full-range; only the detector ignores highs, so transients trigger less.
It's tempting to think an event logger doubles as the program recorder. In fact it stores a low-resolution reference copy plus a timed log, not a master.
Common belief: dynamic range control and loudness normalization are the same. Actually DRC reshapes the loud-soft gap via optional decoder metadata.
Myth: the lowest THD percentage always means the better-sounding device. Actually THD ignores noise, and figures taken at different levels aren't comparable.
Myth: the Stereo Out is just another aux you can skip. Actually it's the main mix bus; anything not routed there never reaches the final mix.
Common belief: a bad recorded level can always be fixed downstream with makeup gain. Actually that just raises the noise floor along with the signal.
Myth: gigabit and gigabyte mean the same thing. Actually gigabit (Gb) is a network speed, while gigabyte (GB) is a storage size, eight times different.
Myth: a system's calibration reference level is its maximum safe level. Actually it's just the nominal anchor point; headroom above it prevents clipping.
Myth: dialogue gets clearer just by turning it up. Actually raising level alone fights the music; clearing space and boosting consonant range works better.
Myth: earth ground makes gear safe by draining faults into the dirt. Actually safety comes from the bonded low-impedance path back to the source, not the earth.
Myth: tom mics only need good placement, nothing else. Actually ignoring their polarity relative to the overheads can thin out the whole kit once channels sum.
Myth: silver-plated cable lowers resistance at audio frequencies. Actually that benefit only shows up at radio frequencies, where skin effect matters.
Myth: specific loudness numbers are already loudness in sones. Actually it's a density, loudness per frequency slice, summed to get total loudness.
Myth: any filter with a 24 dB/octave slope is Linkwitz-Riley. Actually slope alone doesn't define it - LR-4 cascades two Butterworth stages to sum flat.
Myth: all MEMS microphones are capacitive and need a bias voltage. Actually piezoelectric MEMS mics sense bending stress directly, with no bias or backplate.
Myth: acoustic contrast control faithfully reproduces the target sound in the bright zone. Actually it maximizes the loudness ratio between zones instead.
The myth: PAPR uses 20 log, like a voltage ratio. Actually it compares power to power, so it uses 10 log — 20 log doubles the dB value.
Widely believed: clipping early in the chain washes out once you turn things down later. Really, that distortion just gets amplified with everything else.
Common belief: checking peak meters is enough QC before release. Actually integrated loudness (LUFS) against a platform target is what really needs checking.
Play an old optical film track through a flat modern chain expecting balance. The Academy curve rolls off highs and lows -- flat playback sounds thin and hissy.
Myth: a transmitter's input level and its RF output power are the same setting. Actually they're separate - input level sets audio drive, RF sets range.
Myth: a supercardioid rejects all sound from behind. Actually it has a rear lobe about 10 dB down — its true nulls sit at the sides.
The myth: a cable that passes a continuity test is guaranteed reliable. Actually it can still fail under flexing unless you wiggle the connectors while testing.
The myth: ceiling baffles are rated like flat wall panels. Both faces absorb, so baffles are rated by absorption area per unit, not a surface coefficient.
Myth: ultrasound is a different kind of wave than normal sound. Actually it's just sound above 20 kHz, obeying the same physics, but fading fast in air.
Myth: matching peak levels across an album's tracks makes them feel consistent. Actually perceived loudness, not peak level, is what needs matching.
Myth: an amplifier's gain knob is just another volume control. Actually gain matches input sensitivity to the source's max output; cranking it invites clipping.
Popular belief: convolution reverb can be freely reshaped like an algorithmic reverb's decay. Actually it's locked to whatever impulse response you captured.
The myth: any long control signal works fine as a sequencer reset. Actually a held gate keeps it stuck in reset; it needs a short trigger pulse to restart.
Studio myth: someone with recruitment is just exaggerating when loud sounds bother them. Actually it's a real cochlear effect; loudness grows abnormally fast.
Common belief: a horn's throat resistance stays flat above its cutoff frequency. Actually it climbs from zero at cutoff toward its maximum well above it.
Myth: 'analytical' sound is always the better, more accurate choice. Actually it often implies a cold, fatiguing character — detail at the cost of warmth.

term: Gain staging through a recording chain
body: Myth: a fader can undo a badly set input gain. Once a stage clips or buries a signal in noise, nothing downstream in the chain can recover it.
Myth: adding more output level fixes uneven sound-system coverage. Turning it up just makes the whole uneven pattern louder -- it doesn't even out the seats.
The myth: quantization and sampling are the same step. Actually sampling discretizes time while quantization rounds amplitude — two separate operations.
The myth: loudness enhancement proves a preceding tone genuinely boosts the one after it. Actually much of the effect is the comparison tone being reduced.
Myth: a quarter-inch measurement mic is just a smaller half-inch mic. Actually its small diaphragm trades sensitivity for higher SPL and HF range.
Pairing in-ears with a wedge keeps all the hearing-safety benefit of in-ears alone? Not quite — a loud wedge still adds to your total exposure.
Widely believed: it doesn't matter what drives a reverb ducker's sidechain. Really, keying it from the wet reverb instead of the dry source defeats the effect.
The myth: a bulk-erased blank tape is perfectly silent. Actually the demagnetized coating still has its own random-magnetization noise floor.
Popular belief: fipple and labium name the same part. Actually the fipple is the block that shapes the air jet; the labium is the sharp edge that jet strikes.
Common belief: constant-power panning keeps a centered source level when summed to mono. Actually mono summing can make it rise about 3 dB instead.
Popular belief: the Glyn Johns method is a standard spaced overhead pair. Actually the trick is measuring both mics exactly equidistant from the snare.
Myth: 'balanced armature' and 'balanced' audio line are related. Actually they're unrelated - one's a tiny magnetic transducer, the other differential wiring.
Popular belief: a higher bass ratio always makes a better hall. Actually it only signals more low-frequency reverb versus mids; desirable depends on the music.
Is the 3 dB down point where a filter's output stops entirely? Not quite - it just marks the half-power edge; response continues well past it.
Myth: two signals with the same peak reading are equally loud. Loudness tracks average (RMS) energy, so the denser signal always sounds louder.
Myth: a broadcast limiter's main job is to raise loudness. Actually it exists to prevent overmodulation of the transmitter - loudness is a side effect.
Myth: peaks reading safely below 0 dBFS guarantee a clean encode. Inter-sample true peaks can still clip after MP3 or AAC conversion, sample peaks or not.
Myth: an electret condenser mic needs no power since its charge is built in. Actually its internal FET preamp still needs battery or phantom power to run.
Myth: PFL and AFL both reflect the fader position. Actually PFL taps before the fader, so it's heard at full level even faded down.
It's tempting to think acoustic sensing always sends out a sound to get a reading. In fact many systems only listen passively, emitting nothing.
Myth: a mirrored backup console copies every setting automatically. Actually input gain, phantom power, and pad must still be set separately on each desk.
Widely believed: a DAC just outputs the raw sample numbers as sound. Really, it reconstructs them through a filter — skip that and you'd hear stepped noise.
Myth: speaker coupling holds no matter how far apart the sources sit. Actually it needs close spacing; space subs a wavelength apart and they decouple.
Myth: an RMS detector tracks the same thing as a peak detector. Averaging detection follows the signal's mean power, which tracks loudness, not instant peaks.
Studio myth: proximity effect's boomy low end has to be fixed with EQ after. Actually it's better managed at the source, with placement or a filter.
Common belief: any volume knob works fine regardless of its taper. Actually a linear-taper pot on a level control bunches most change into a few degrees.
Myth: foam panels absorb deep bass just like they absorb highs. Actually porous absorbers need real thickness or an air gap before they touch low frequencies.
Myth: the mix position tells you what the whole room hears. The front row sits in the harshest, loudest seats - walk there and check before doors.
Myth: if sound isn't painful yet, it's a safe level. Actually hearing damage sets in far below the 120-140 dB pain threshold - pain isn't the safety line.
It's tempting to think gating artificially lowers a loudness reading. In fact it just excludes silent blocks so pauses don't skew the average.
The myth: a keyboard amp colors tone the way a guitar amp does. Actually it aims for a wide, flat response to reproduce the keyboard's own sound accurately.
Common belief: making everything loud enough creates a cohesive mix. Actually cohesion comes from matching tone, dynamics, and space, not loudness.
Myth: matching a wide shot's perspective just means turning dialogue down. Actually level alone leaves it sounding close and dry; EQ and reverb must move too.
Common belief: a hotter output level always means better sound. Actually driving it too high just clips the very next input's maximum level.
Myth: a wavefront is a ray pointing outward from the source. Actually it's a surface of constant phase, perpendicular to the direction rays travel.
Popular belief: a 'darker' sound just means lower pitch. Actually timbre comes from harmonic content and envelope - same pitch, same loudness, different color.
Common belief: an op-amp delivers its full gain at every frequency. Actually gain falls as frequency rises, reaching zero (unity) at its gain-bandwidth product.
Studio myth: one number is the reference monitoring level for every room. Actually smaller rooms typically calibrate to a lower target SPL.
Myth: tape saturation works like a compressor's threshold-triggered gain reduction. Actually it's a gradual softening as level nears magnetic saturation.
Commonly assumed: a file's loudness and peak metadata stay valid after you edit or transcode it — but any change can make old metadata stale and untrustworthy.
Myth: a 24-bit converter delivers its full theoretical dynamic range. Real analog noise floors always fall short of the ideal 6.02 dB-per-bit figure.
Myth: close miking alone gives a recording depth. Actually depth comes from the room's reflected sound; close mics capture mostly direct signal, not ambience.
It's tempting to assume matched monitor speakers sound equally loud out of the box. Trim each output separately, ideally with pink noise and an SPL meter.
A 24-bit converter delivers its full 144 dB of dynamic range? Not quite — analog noise limits real converters to roughly 120 dB, spec sheets aside.
Studio myth: faders always show channel levels. In flip (sends-on-faders) mode they set send levels to one mix - forget that, and you 'fix' the wrong mix.
Myth: wider FM deviation is always better. Actually it only improves signal-to-noise by widening the channel, so fewer systems fit in the band.
Myth: a tilt or pivot EQ is just a single boost control. Actually it always cuts the opposite side of the pivot too; brightening one end darkens the other.
Myth: a good crowd bed is a loud crowd bed. One clear word breaks the spell - the craft is an anonymous wash that supports dialogue without competing.
Myth: a 'polycarbonate' replacement capacitor is the real thing. Actually true polycarbonate film is largely discontinued, so most use another dielectric.
The myth: a sustain pedal working backwards must be broken. Actually it's usually a polarity mismatch between pedal and keyboard.
The myth: a signal fault is probably a bad cable. Trace the path stage by stage with a test signal first -- routing and gain errors are just as common a cause.
Myth: an input attenuator changes an amp's max output power. Actually it only changes sensitivity — how much input reaches that same fixed ceiling.
Myth: if the fader's up, the channel is in the mix. Routing decides that - an unassigned channel reaches no bus, however loud the fader says.
Studio myth: a flat-top clipped waveform can be fully restored. Actually the peak info is gone, replaced by added harmonic distortion, and can't be undone.
Common belief: two mics of one model are already matched. Actually unit variation shifts sensitivity — matching means tuning pairs to a tight tolerance.
Commonly assumed: setting a limiter's ceiling at 0 dBFS is safe — but lossy encoding and sample-rate conversion can push true peaks above full scale afterward.
The myth: riding the gain means moving the fader. Actually it's adjusting input trim in real time, which changes the signal feeding everything downstream.
Studio myth: judging bass at one loud level tells you the true balance. Actually equal-loudness hearing shifts with volume, so balance can sound wrong softer.
Myth: one impulse response captures a room. It captures one source-and-mic geometry - and run fully wet it drowns dialogue instead of placing it.
Myth: music carries the same small crest factor as a steady sine wave. Actually speech and music have much taller peaks above average, often 12-20 dB higher.
Popular belief: a 'dry' monitor mix means a quiet or thin one. Actually dry just means no added reverb or delay — level and fullness are separate matters.
Myth: DC offset is something you can hear directly in a signal. Actually it's inaudible by itself; the real problems are wasted headroom and clicks at edits.
Common belief: a driver's thermal resistance is basically its electrical resistance. Actually it's a separate heat-path rating that sets how hot the coil runs.
Myth: aim a hi-hat mic straight at the cymbal's edge gap. Actually that blasts air into the capsule on every hit; angle it away, over the top.
Common belief: an organ's swell pedal changes the whole instrument's volume. Actually it only opens shutters on divisions enclosed in a swell box.
Myth: an amp's clip limiter adds extra power or loudness. Actually it only holds the signal just below clipping to protect drivers, not to boost output.
Common belief: bypassing system limiters just unlocks more volume. Actually they cap output at rated limits to stop drivers and amps from destructive damage.
Widely believed: pro and consumer nominal levels are interchangeable. Actually +4 dBu and -10 dBV differ by roughly 12 dB.
Common belief: a phaser's notches are evenly spaced like a flanger's. Actually its all-pass stages create non-harmonic notches, unlike delay-based flanging.
Commonly assumed: a mandolin's bridge pickup sounds just like a mic on the instrument — but it senses bridge vibration alone, giving a tight, quacky tone.
The myth: a reverb send needs some dry signal mixed back in to sound right. Actually the channel already carries the dry sound, so the return can run fully wet.
It's tempting to think fixed-point math has floating point's huge headroom. In fact its range is fixed, so loud sums can overflow and clip.
Studio myth: any ported box counts as 'tuned' just because it has a port. Actually a true alignment matches box volume, port tuning, and driver Q together.
Common belief: a port's inertance depends only on its physical length. Actually you need the effective length, which includes end corrections beyond the tube.
Myth: a flat frequency response guarantees accurate transient reproduction. Magnitude response alone ignores phase, which also shapes how transients arrive.
Myth: two microphones of the same model have identical sensitivity. Actually each unit can differ within its rated tolerance, a real concern for matched pairs.
Myth: surround channels calibrate to the same 85 dB SPL as the screens. Actually surrounds are set 3 dB lower, at 82 dB SPL, in theatrical alignment.
The myth: a phasey, hollow sound is just dullness or bad EQ. Actually it's cancellation from combining two versions of one signal - EQ alone won't fix it.
Common belief: peak sound pressure and RMS SPL are the same number. Actually RMS averages the signal's power, so reporting a peak as RMS overstates the level.
Myth: the channel fader can fix a poorly set preamp gain. Actually a bad trim sets the noise floor or clipping point before the fader ever gets a chance.
Myth: presence and air are the same high-frequency boost. Actually presence (4-6 kHz) adds intelligibility and forwardness, while air sits much higher.
Myth: any quick break lets tired ears recover. Actually side-of-stage or a loud bar doesn't work — real recovery needs actual quiet, and it isn't instant.
Myth: harsh and bright are the same complaint. Actually harshness is aggressive 2-5 kHz energy or distortion; bright is extended, pleasant highs.
The myth: troubleshooting a broadcast chain works fine at random. Actually following it in order from source to transmitter finds faults faster.
Myth: two sounds at the same SPL are equally loud. Actually total loudness depends on spectrum and bandwidth too; it's summed in sones, not read off a dB meter.
Common belief: an electret's permanent charge lasts forever. Actually it can slowly leak away over decades — why old capsules eventually need replacing.
Myth: a higher dBFS peak reading means a track sounds louder. Actually loudness also depends on frequency content and duration, not amplitude alone.
Popular belief: clipping a signal just makes it louder. Actually hard clipping mainly adds harsh, high-order harmonic distortion, and can overheat tweeters.
Myth: a very low meter reading always means the room is genuinely quiet. Actually below the meter's own noise floor, an under-range warning means invalid.
Myth: every kill switch cuts a band to total silence. Actually some only attenuate to around -26 dB, not negative infinity.
Myth: RMS level and the plain average of a signal are the same thing. Actually RMS squares the values first, so it tracks power, unlike a simple average.
Myth: any driver can be forced into a maximally flat Butterworth box alignment. Actually a B4 vented alignment needs a driver with total Q near 0.383.

term: Export bit depth versus processing bit depth
body: Myth: exporting at 16-bit sounds worse because the mix wasn't 'processed' at 16-bit. The DAW mixes in high-precision float regardless -- just dither going down.
Commonly assumed: AGC protects a signal from clipping - but it manages average level over time, not instantaneous peaks; a limiter may still be needed.
The myth: turning an amp up further gets you more clean level. Once it's 'out of gas' at its power limit, pushing harder only adds distortion, not volume.
The myth: raising faders can mask a badly gain-staged input. Actually setting inputs first - patching, gain, phantom, phase - is the whole foundation.
The myth: a vari-mu compressor gives fast, surgical transient control. Actually vari-mu units are inherently smooth and program-dependent, not snappy.
Myth: a distortion pedal sounds the same wherever you place it. Actually stacking it after an already-clipping preamp muddies the tone instead of shaping it.
Myth: dynamic range and signal-to-noise ratio are the same metric. Actually it shows the gap between loud and soft; bigger isn't automatically better.
Myth: a cupped, honky vocal is an EQ problem. It's often literal - a hand cupped over the mic grille hollows the mids and kills the open top.
Myth: an isobar's -6 dB line marks an absolute SPL value. Actually it's a relative contour, showing where level drops 6 dB below on-axis, not a fixed loudness.
Myth: a perfectly flat curve on the analyzer guarantees a good mix. Actually it only displays the signal - a flat-looking spectrum can still sound wrong.
The myth: carpet or thin foam makes a room fully dead. Actually they absorb mainly high frequencies, leaving low-end liveness ringing on underneath.
Commonly assumed: far-field capture stays as clean as close miking — but distance costs signal-to-noise, and reverberation dominates sooner than you'd guess.
The myth: the cinema X curve suits music or live-sound systems too. Actually it's a calibration standard specific to dubbing and theater playback rooms.
Myth: a noisy or distorted signal is a problem at the output stage. Actually it often entered far earlier in the path and just carries through untouched.
Myth: cutting a rotor's thrust or loading reduces its thickness noise. Actually thickness noise depends only on blade volume and tip speed, not on lift.
The 'hot seat' is a specific physical mixing chair? Not quite — it names the exposure of live, irreversible mixing decisions, wherever that engineer sits.
Commonly assumed: organ pipes in a chamber sound as strong as pipes standing openly in the room — but the chamber walls muffle and color the tone considerably.
Myth: dialnorm changes the actual recorded audio. Actually it's metadata only; the decoder reads it and adjusts playback gain, leaving the file untouched.
Myth: stacking speaker boxes vertically automatically makes a true line array. Actually coupling only works if spacing and wavefront-flatness criteria are met.
Myth: a momentary or short-term loudness reading tells you if a program is compliant. Actually only the integrated loudness figure is the real target.
Myth: blending a distorted copy under a dry signal just adds grit for free. Uncorrected phase or latency between the two paths can cancel and thin the sound.
Common belief: a small horn mouth still gives smooth low-frequency response. Actually the impedance mismatch there reflects sound back, rippling the response.
Myth: a trashy-sounding cymbal is a broken or damaged one. Actually trashy is often intentional character, a dense, inharmonic, dirty tone like a china.
Myth: lowering a limiter's ceiling makes the track quieter. Actually input gain sets loudness - the ceiling only caps how high peaks can reach.
Myth: wire recording was an early form of tape. It stored sound magnetically on steel wire, invented decades before coated tape replaced it.
A bright speaker cabinet looks like an EQ problem. Often the horn attenuator (L-pad) is just set too high -- check that before reaching for EQ.
Myth: a papery sound just means it needs more treble. Actually papery describes missing low-end body, so boosting highs alone only makes it thinner.
Myth: any tape can use the same bias setting. Actually bias current must be calibrated for each tape formulation and speed, or distortion and noise suffer.
Commonly assumed: plug-in power is the same as 48V phantom power - but it's only a few volts through a mini-jack, and can't run a studio condenser mic.
The myth: a sound-system prediction plane is measured at floor level. Actually it's mapped at listener ear height across the seating area, not the floor.
A modulation monitor can run off any program feed? Not quite — it must sample the transmitter's real output; a studio-side feed defeats its purpose.
It's tempting to think a phone SPL app is fine for compliance checks. In fact only a calibrated meter is reliable — one peak reading understates exposure.
Myth: a brass mute just makes things quieter. A straight mute rewrites the timbre - thin, buzzy, edgy - which is why it counts as a sound, not a volume.
Studio myth: renaming a channel's scribble strip changes its routing. It's only a label -- updating it never moves or reassigns the actual signal.
Myth: analyzer bands are all equally wide. Fractional-octave bands are constant percentage - they widen in hertz as frequency climbs, unlike FFT bins.
Myth: adding more presence or treble EQ fixes a fizzy tone. Actually that excess energy already sits in the 4-10 kHz range, so boosting there makes fizz worse.
Studio myth: a flat frequency response means a filter leaves the waveform untouched. Actually phase shift still varies by frequency, reshaping transients.
Myth: a digital-ready master sounds fine dropped onto cassette. Actually tape can't reproduce those extremes cleanly - it needs its own tailored master.
Popular belief: a high shelf and a high-pass filter do the same thing. Actually a shelf levels off into a flat plateau; a high-pass keeps cutting steadily.
Myth: a panel glued flat to the wall absorbs bass as well as one spaced off it. Actually no air gap behind it cuts low-frequency absorption noticeably.
Myth: if a reference track sounds better, it must actually be better. Actually mismatched comparison levels can make the louder track win on loudness alone.
Widely believed: +20 dB means 100 times the pressure. Really, that's the power view; for pressure, +20 dB is only 10 times, since pressure uses 20 log10.
Common belief: a venue's main array reaches every seat, even under a balcony. Actually the overhang blocks that path — fills are needed to cover it.
Myth: plucking with the nail is just louder. The hard nail releases the string faster, adding high partials - it's brighter, not merely stronger.
Common belief: semitone steps are equal in hertz across the keyboard. Actually they're equal in ratio, so the hertz gap widens as pitch rises.
The myth: monitor calibration just means setting one volume level. Actually it needs the right meter weighting too, or the level reads wrong.
Myth: miking straight at an acoustic guitar's sound hole gives the truest tone. It mostly captures a boomy resonance, not the whole instrument's balance.
Myth: open-back headphones isolate sound like closed ones. Actually their vented design leaks sound both in and out, so they suit quiet rooms only.
Common belief: all analog meters share the same pivot-and-jewel movement. Actually a taut-band meter suspends its coil on tensioned ribbons, removing friction.
Digital radio needs the same pre-emphasis and hard clipping as analog FM? Not quite — it skips FM pre-emphasis; it's built for a codec, not an RF path.
Myth: a mix that sounds clean on one system is free of distortion. Actually clipping and true-peak overs can hide there; check meters and a second monitor too.
The myth: a blackburst signal carries picture information. Actually its image is just black; its value is the sync and timing it locks other gear to.
The myth: a hyped, smile-EQ sound is just accurate audio that sounds exciting. Actually it's boosted lows and highs with scooped mids - exciting, not accurate.
Myth: a cold ending just means a fast fade-out. Actually it's the opposite; the band stops dead together on a chord, no tapering at all.
Myth: your meter always shows the true peak reaching overload. Actually many meters miss fast peaks, so gain can pass overload with no warning.
Myth: a flickering clip light is always harmless. In a power amplifier stage, sustained clipping can damage the drivers it's feeding.
Myth: separating clashing instruments means boosting each one's frequencies. Actually cutting from whichever needs it least makes room without losing headroom.
Myth: you sing into the top of a big studio condenser. Side-address mics listen through their broad face - usually the logo side - not the end.
Myth: thin foam fixes a boxy-sounding vocal booth. Actually foam does little at low frequencies, so the modal boxiness usually remains.
Myth: a safe average dBA reading means a show is safe throughout. Actually momentary peaks can still damage hearing even when the average stays within limits.
Myth: clicks and dropouts on networked audio mean a bad converter or gain stage. Actually they're often lost or late Ethernet packets, not an analog fault.
Myth: the Harman target is a perfectly flat response. Actually it's flat through the midrange with a gentle downward tilt toward the treble.
Common belief: any compressor preserves transients equally. Actually a fast attack clamps the punch, so this technique relies on a slower attack instead.
Myth: headphone level and input gain are the same control. Actually confusing the two means cranking input gain for more volume, which can overdrive the input.
Studio myth: peak-to-peak amplitude always equals twice the peak. Actually that only holds for a symmetric waveform; an asymmetric wave breaks the rule.
The myth: amplifier monitoring software can fix a fault. Actually it only reports status like temperature and level - repairs still happen at the rack.
Myth: level-matching speakers by ear is close enough. Actually trim calibration needs a calibrated SPL meter and a defined pink-noise reference.
Myth: making every element fully 3D sounds more immersive. Push everything to full spatial positioning and you lose the stable, enveloping background.
The cinema 'wide-range' curve suits any room? Not quite — its high-frequency roll-off is tuned for large cinemas; applying it small just darkens the sound.
Myth: a bigger damping-factor number always means tighter bass. Actually once cable and coil resistance dominate, huge numbers add little.
Myth: plate reverb sounds naturally dark. Actually it's characteristically bright and dense, with no distinct early reflections like a real room has.
Widely believed: pin 2 is always 'hot' on every device. Really, older or non-standard gear can wire it differently, flipping polarity against other mics.
A bad-sounding monitor mix means broken gear or a bad cable? Not quite — the signal may be fine; it's often just routed from the wrong mix bus entirely.
Myth: an output level trim is the same as input gain. Trim fine-tunes what leaves a device to match the next input, not where you fix an upstream problem.
It's tempting to think every multi-pattern condenser mic switches pattern on its body. In fact many tube and remote mics switch only at the power supply.
Popular belief: fine gain trim can rescue a badly set preamp gain. Actually it only fine-tunes level - the coarse gain stage needs correcting first.
Common belief: a muddy mix needs more treble to clear up. Actually muddiness is excess low-mid buildup; boosting highs won't fix it, cutting low-mids will.
Popular belief: an EQ boost adds new content to a signal. Actually it only amplifies frequencies already present, and it carries phase changes the graph hides.
Myth: a pistonphone's calibration level is the mic's usable SPL ceiling. Actually it's just one fixed reference tone; the mic's real max SPL is unrelated.
Myth: a bigger tape-head gap always gives better output. Actually gap length trades off with high-frequency response; too large a gap loses highs on playback.
Widely believed: phantom power is safe for any condenser mic. Many ribbon mics can be damaged by 48V, especially if patched in while it's live.
You delay the farther speaker to line things up? Not quite — you hold back the closer source, since it arrives first and needs the delay.
The myth: pulling the master fader down fixes a hot channel. It only lowers everything together -- excess gain upstream is still there, just quieter.
Myth: 'A' always means the log, audio taper. Actually some older or regional parts reverse the A and B labeling convention, so it isn't universal.
Myth: every stage wedge carries its own individual mix. Actually many are fed from one shared aux; two performers can be hearing the identical blend.
Myth: turning the main monitor knob down works like hitting DIM. Actually DIM drops a fixed amount and restores it exactly - the knob loses your reference.
Myth: one bias setting works for every tape. Actually different formulations need different bias current, set during machine alignment.
A mix that sounds great on studio monitors will translate fine on-air? Not quite — broadcast processing and tiny TV speakers can shrink it thin and weak.
Myth: a larger mic diaphragm is simply the better choice. Actually large diaphragms turn directional off-axis at high frequency; small ones stay uniform.
The myth: round-trip latency is just the interface's single buffer delay. Actually input, output, converter, and plug-in delays all add up.
Myth: a daily listening check keeps an audiometer fully calibrated. Actually only an annual electroacoustic calibration verifies distortion and linearity too.
Widely believed: a horn amplifies power like an amplifier does. Really, it only transforms impedance, matching a driver to open air - no power added.
Studio myth: a MIDI controller makes sound by itself. Actually it only sends note and control data — a synth or software makes the actual sound.
Myth: a raised hearing threshold means a raised discomfort level too. Actually in cochlear loss discomfort level often stays normal, narrowing the usable range.
Widely assumed: silence from a condenser mic means it's dead. Often it's just a broken cable or missing phantom power, not the microphone itself.
Myth: equal-loudness contours keep the same shape at every volume. They flatten at high levels -- the ear's uneven bass/treble response is strongest when quiet.
Myth: a 'silent' practice guitar makes no sound without headphones. Actually the strings still produce a faint acoustic sound; silent just means quiet.
Myth: a Butterworth crossover always sums perfectly flat. Actually even-order versions actually peak +3 dB right at the crossover frequency.
Myth: a dead note and a ghost note are the same thing. Actually a ghost note is quiet but still pitched, while a dead note is a muted, pitchless thud.
Myth: checking peak level is enough to pass loudness compliance. Actually delivery specs like R128 grade the whole program's integrated LUFS.
Popular belief: recovering a power ratio from decibels means dividing by 20, like pressure. Actually power uses 10 log10, so you divide by 10, not 20.
A capsule's two diaphragms are automatically identical? Not quite — manufacturing variation means they often need selecting or trimming to match.
Myth: boosting the highs makes a sound silky. Actually silky means smooth, refined treble with no harshness - piling on brightness adds harshness instead.
The myth: RMS always equals 0.707 times a signal's peak. Actually that factor only holds for a pure sine wave; other waveforms have a different ratio.
Common belief: 'wet' means the final wet/dry blend. Actually wet refers only to the effected signal itself - the mixed result is a separate thing.
Myth: leaving both hardware and software monitoring on just gives you a safety backup. Actually hearing both at once creates a doubled, flanged sound.
Myth: a low THD reading at moderate volume means a mic stays clean at its loudest. Actually distortion climbs sharply near a mic's maximum SPL.
Studio myth: a bright mix is just a loud one. Actually brightness is a high-frequency tonal balance, unrelated to overall level.
Myth: a sharp-sounding tone must also be loud. Actually sharpness tracks high-frequency content, not level - a quiet sound can still feel sharp.
Myth: a compact console's small fader count is its total channel count. Actually digital compacts often access far more channels via layers and banking.
Myth: winding tape as tightly as possible is always safest. Over-tight winds can stretch or emboss the tape -- and heads-out storage worsens print-through.
Myth: a subcardioid mic rejects the rear like a cardioid does. Actually it only attenuates it by 6-10 dB, far weaker than a true cardioid null.
Myth: warm tilt just means a narrow bass boost. Actually it's a broad, gentle downward slope from bass to treble, not a bump at one frequency.
Myth: boosting sub-bass makes guitar chugs heavier. Actually that just muddies the mix; a chug's punch comes from palm-muted damping, not added low end.
Myth: a resonator pickup plugs straight into any input at full tone. Actually a bridge piezo needs a high-impedance preamp or DI, or it sounds thin.
The myth: the broadcast mix and the streaming mix share one loudness target. Actually each outlet has its own spec, so broadcast gets reconformed separately.
Myth: the least significant bit is just noise. Actually it carries real low-level detail; truncating it without dither audibly distorts quiet passages.
Common belief: decoding a noise-reduction tape later is as accurate as decoding at transfer. Actually alignment errors can compound the longer decoding waits.
Myth: a word's lexical stress is just about saying it louder. Actually duration, pitch movement, and full vowel quality often carry more of the contrast.
Myth: a quieter design can beat the thermal noise of its own source resistance. Actually that noise floor is set by resistance and temperature alone.
Common belief: an amplifier's residual-noise reading is valid with the input open. Actually it must be terminated, or the reading is inflated.
The myth: one loudness target fits every broadcaster. Actually each outlet sets its own loudness and true-peak spec - peak meters alone won't confirm delivery.
Myth: sending a channel to two mix buses is always harmless. Actually if those buses recombine downstream, the signal doubles and can comb-filter.
Myth: resting your hand on the djembe head after a bass stroke sounds fine. Actually it damps the note; let the hand rebound so the deep tone rings out.
Myth: distortion is distortion. Second-order harmonics read sweet and musical; third-order reads harsh and edgy - the mix of the two is the character.
Myth: saturation can replace solid level and EQ balance on bass. Actually it just adds warmth — pushing it to compensate turns the low end fuzzy.
Common belief: signal-to-distortion ratio is signal-to-noise ratio. Actually it weighs harmonic and intermod content, not noise, and drops as level rises.
The myth: a speaker's coverage angle stays the same at every frequency. Actually beamwidth typically narrows up high, and the plot shows exactly where.
Myth: the main hook usually lives in the verse. Actually verses reuse the same melody with new lyrics each time and set up the hook, which lands in the chorus.
Myth: a louder car stereo scores better in an SQ competition. Actually loudness belongs to a separate contest; judges reward tonal accuracy instead.
Popular belief: every mixer, digital included, has a physical summing amplifier. Actually digital consoles sum by adding sample values - no analog amp involved.
The myth: silent gaps between dialogue lines are inaudible in the mix. Actually true digital silence makes the noise floor jump - room tone must fill every gap.
Common belief: 'squashed' just means a dense, busy arrangement. Actually it means heavy compression flattened dynamic range, killing punch.
The myth: more input gain means more maximum power. Actually gain only sets sensitivity, not the amp's rated output ceiling.
Common belief: a PZM works like any small mic just set on a table. Actually move it off the boundary and its whole cancellation-avoiding design falls apart.
Common belief: a drum bus is fine as long as the master fader doesn't clip. Actually the bus itself can clip earlier in the chain, before the master shows it.
Myth: YUV, YPbPr, and YCbCr all mean the same thing. Actually they're distinct analog and digital variants of the same luma/chroma idea, not interchangeable.
Myth: mic capsules are interchangeable, so any mic will do the job. Actually the capsule type and design - dynamic, condenser, ribbon - defines the sound.
Studio myth: pre-drop silence needs to be dead quiet to work. A hard cut can click -- a short fade or a low-level tail often builds the tension just as well.
Myth: cascading amplifier stages just adds up their dB noise figures. Actually the first stage dominates total system noise; later stages matter far less.
Myth: white noise sounds tonally even like pink noise. Actually white carries more power per octave as pitch rises, so it sounds bright and hissy.
Myth: the threshold of hearing is one fixed sound level. Actually it's a curve that shifts with frequency, most sensitive near 3-4 kHz.
Popular belief: a 'colored' sound is always a flaw. Actually many prized mics and preamps are loved precisely for their pleasant coloration.
Myth: 0 dBr is a fixed voltage like dBu or dBV. The r means relative - it marks whatever reference this test chose, so its value changes per test.
Common belief: a standard linear crossfader is dipless. Actually a linear blend drops volume at the midpoint; dipless needs a constant-power curve.
Myth: a loud, limited streaming master will cut to vinyl just fine. Actually vinyl needs its own pre-master - tamed sibilance, centered bass, lower level.
Myth: pushing a track as loud as possible pays off. Actually streaming normalization turns it back down anyway, leaving you with crushed dynamics for nothing.
Myth: power gain in dB always uses the 20-times-log formula. Actually that's for voltage - power gain in dB uses ten times the log of the ratio.
Widely believed: 'dry' means completely unprocessed. Really, it only means no added reverb - EQ and compression can still apply.
Popular belief: glassy sheen is always a compliment. A little reads clear and sparkly; chase it with high boosts and the sound turns cold and brittle.
Popular belief: a 'dead' room has no bass problems since it has no echo. Actually low frequencies can still build up even in a heavily absorbed room.
Studio myth: octave-band levels add up by simple arithmetic in dB. Actually they must be summed on an energy (mean-square) basis, not added directly.
The myth: the soundcheck mix will sound the same once the room's packed. Actually a loud, full audience changes everything, so it needs fast rebalancing.
Myth: max output level and saturation level are the same tape spec. Actually max output uses a 3% distortion criterion; saturation has no distortion criterion.
Myth: categorical loudness units (CU) are basically decibels. Actually they're a perceptual rating scale built from listener judgments, not a physical level.
Cranking trigger gain to catch weak hits sounds harmless. Set too high, it also picks up crosstalk and light taps as false, stuck-loud triggers.
Myth: two sounds judged equally loud must be set to equal level. In a loudness-balance test the matched levels usually differ -- that gap is the whole point.
Myth: a metallic, ringing tone means the source itself is bad. Actually it often comes from reverb ringing, aliasing, or clipping, not the original sound.
Myth: 'discrete' means separate channels. Actually it means an amp built from individual transistors and resistors, not a single IC chip.
Myth: your average signal level is the same as its peak level. Actually headroom is measured against the peaks; assuming they match invites unexpected clipping.
Studio myth: any circuit that passes signal is fine for audio use. Actually audio-grade circuits need deliberately low noise and real headroom.
Myth: an internal guitar mic can run wide open at any volume. Actually pushing it too hot invites feedback; the pickup should carry more as level rises.
Myth: -18 dBFS and -20 dBFS references are interchangeable. EBU and SMPTE pick different points, and mismatching them misaligns headroom between facilities.
Myth: an output channel strip works like an input strip for one mic. Actually it controls the final summed bus feeding your speakers, not a single source.
The myth: steel strings are a fine upgrade for a nylon-string guitar. Actually the far higher tension can damage its lighter bracing, built for nylon only.
Myth: the speed of sound is a fixed number. Actually it rises with air temperature and is much faster still through water or solids.
Myth: digital full scale behaves like analog overload, adding pleasant saturation. Actually digital clips hard and instantly at 0 dBFS, with no soft overshoot.
Myth: a drive knob just controls output volume. Actually drive pushes the input into overload for saturation; output level is a separate control.
Myth: only digital signals can clip. Actually analog stages clip too; hard clipping truncates peaks abruptly while soft clipping rounds them more gently.
The myth: doubling bit depth doubles the number of quantization levels. Actually levels equal two to the bit count — one extra bit doubles them.
Popular belief: pre-delay at zero is the neutral, default setting. Actually zero pre-delay lets the reverb smear straight into the source, reducing clarity.
Myth: sound sources radiate as flat, plane waves. Actually near a small source the wavefront curves like an expanding bubble; only far away does it flatten.
Myth: a veiled sound needs a high boost. The veil usually comes from masking or over-compression - fix the cause, or the boost just adds harshness on top.
Myth: a warm, bassy vocal sound comes from the microphone itself. Move a directional mic close to the source and proximity effect boosts the low end on its own.
Myth: hitting the loudness target automatically keeps true peaks safe. Actually the target and the true-peak ceiling are separate limits, both need watching.
Myth: any wireless transmitter and receiver pair sounds fine together. Mismatched compander schemes garble dynamics -- both ends need the same compression law.
Myth: a wider air gap in a condenser capsule gives more output. Actually capacitance rises as the gap shrinks, so a narrower gap means higher sensitivity.
Myth: a guitar amp should sound clean and neutral like hi-fi gear. Actually it's voiced to shape tone and add character, even distortion, on purpose.
Myth: distance factor means more loudness working farther away. Actually it preserves the direct-to-reverberant ratio, not level.
Studio myth: I2S and I2C are the same bus. Actually I2S carries digital audio over three lines; I2C is an unrelated chip-control bus with a different job.
Common belief: a flat magnitude response means a filter adds no timing distortion. Actually group delay can still vary with frequency, smearing transients.
The myth: matching speaker levels is all immersive calibration needs. Actually skipping time delay leaves overhead and surround images smeared.
Common belief: automation should smooth out a performer's crescendo for consistency. Actually good automation supports the natural build, not overrides it.
A high-shelf filter is basically a high-pass? Not quite — a shelf lifts or cuts everything above its corner; a high-pass removes what's below it.
Myth: air-chain verification just checks audio is present. Actually it confirms every stage also meets its level and loudness targets.
Common belief: every TRS jack carries a balanced mono signal. Actually TRS just as often carries unbalanced stereo — tip left, ring right.
Popular belief: a mic's published on-axis curve describes how it sounds in a room. Actually that curve ignores off-axis color, distance, and reflections.
Widely believed: one loudness target fits every service. Music, podcast, and broadcast platforms each set their own LUFS target and true-peak ceiling.
Myth: EBU R128 replaces ITU-R BS.1770. Actually R128 uses BS.1770 to do the measuring — it just sets the -23 LUFS target and -1 dBTP ceiling.
Myth: the cinema 85 dB per-channel reference applies unchanged to a small home or near-field room. Actually smaller rooms calibrate differently.
Myth: setting gain while a performer plays softly during soundcheck is good enough. Actually it will clip once they hit full performance level.
The myth: soft clipping adds no distortion, unlike hard clipping. It still adds harmonics -- just gentler, lower-order ones instead of harsh high-order content.
Common belief: a dry signal sounds dead or dull. Actually dry just means no added reverb or delay; the raw source can still sound full and lively.
The myth: scratch-pad edits automatically update the main timeline. Actually it's a separate space — finished ideas must be moved back by hand.
Myth: making a part speak in a mix just means turning it up. Actually clarity comes more from transient and presence detail than from raw level.
Myth: a speaker cone moves as one rigid piston across its entire range. Actually above a certain point the cone flexes and breaks up.
Widely believed: parallel compression needs a special kind of compressor. Really, it's just routing - blend a heavily compressed copy with the dry signal.
Myth: aiming a mic straight into an f-hole captures more body. Actually f-holes radiate one strong low resonance, so pointing at one just sounds boomy.
Myth: an impedance-balanced output's cold pin carries an inverted signal. Actually it's just grounded through a matching resistor - only hot carries audio.
Common belief: a boundary mic needs no power since it sits without a stand. Actually a condenser boundary mic still needs phantom power to work at all.
Myth: a 'dry' voice track means it's quiet or low quality. Actually dry just means unprocessed — it can still be loud and pristine.
The myth: a pressure antinode is where air moves the most. Actually pressure swings peak there while air velocity is at its minimum, near rigid walls.
Myth: drum saturation is the same as turning up clean gain. Actually it adds harmonic distortion for perceived loudness and warmth, not just level.
Studio myth: 'punchy' just means loud. Actually punch comes from strong, preserved transients and tight low-mid dynamics, not sheer volume.
The myth: one input range setting works for every signal. Actually too low clips peaks and too high buries quiet signal in noise; it must match the source.
Studio myth: set gain to the average level of a source. Transient peaks sit well above that average, so gain staged to average headroom clips them.
Myth: blending pickup and mic signals always fills out an instrument's tone. Actually without checking phase, the two can cancel and thin the sound instead.
Myth: any tape reaches reference level at the same record setting. Actually formulations differ in sensitivity, so each tape needs its own calibrated trim.
Myth: a track's dynamic contour is just one note's envelope. Actually it also describes the rise and fall of loudness across a whole phrase or arrangement.
Myth: soundcheck levels predict what the show needs. Actually real show level runs louder as the crowd and energy build, so tight soundcheck mixing clips.
