Myth: losing crest factor to compression is basically inaudible. Actually a smaller peak-to-RMS gap changes how transients and loudness are perceived.
Studio myth: wiring two pickups in parallel gives a louder, fatter tone. Actually parallel is brighter and lower-output; series is the fat, loud option.
The myth: any huge hit works as an anthem for any crowd. Actually an anthem's power is crowd-specific; one room's peak moment can fall flat for another.
Studio myth: dBW and dBm mean the same power reference. Actually dBW references one watt and dBm one milliwatt; the two always differ by exactly 30 decibels.
Myth: any tonal coloration from gear is a flaw to avoid. Actually a mic or preamp's pleasing color is often chosen on purpose, and isn't the same as distortion.
Myth: pushing the master fader past unity fixes a too-quiet mix. Actually that risks clipping the output; the real fix is correcting gain structure upstream.
Common belief: hi-fi means loud and bass-heavy. High fidelity means faithful - clean, low-distortion sound true to the source, not a hyped, exciting one.
Studio myth: the holes in a MEMS mic's backplate are cosmetic. Actually they control air damping, letting the diaphragm above move freely.
Myth: written notes for double bass sound at the pitch shown. Actually the instrument sounds a full octave lower than notated — it transposes by convention.
Myth: a mic's Z-weighted and A-weighted self-noise specs can be compared directly. Actually Z has no roll-off, so it usually reads higher than A-weighted.
It's tempting to think switching a processor in and out fairly shows its effect. In fact added gain alone sounds like improvement unless levels are matched.
Pushing mix-bus peaks to 0 dBFS is fine since mastering handles it? Not quite — that leaves no margin, and true peaks can already overshoot unseen.
Commonly assumed: killing the highs is the same as sweeping a low-pass filter — but it slams one fixed EQ band almost silent, not a gradual filter sweep.
Myth: a meter pinned at the top means the mix is loud and good. It's a clipping warning -- the signal has already run out of headroom.

term: Maximum Sine-Wave Frequency from Slew Rate
body: Myth: an amplifier's top frequency is fixed regardless of volume. Actually slew rate limits it more at higher output, so loud signals distort sooner.
Common belief: a peak limiter can rescue a badly gain-staged system. Actually it only caps instantaneous peaks; it can't fix levels that were wrong to start.
Myth: fixing a weak signal by boosting it later in the chain works fine. Actually that also amplifies noise picked up earlier - fix the gain at the source.
It's tempting to think preamp metadata captures how a preamp sounds. It only logs the model and settings used -- not the actual sonic character.
It's tempting to think gain-bandwidth product is a fixed rule for every op-amp. In fact multi-pole or decompensated parts don't follow that constant-GBW rule.
Myth: an insert reverb and a send/return reverb are the same setup. Actually a send lets many tracks share one reverb with independent wet/dry control.
Myth: watching RMS or average meters is enough to catch clipping. Actually short peaks can clip between readings; true-peak metering actually prevents it.
Myth: two mics at the same fader position are equally loud. Actually differing sensitivities mean identical fader settings yield different levels.
The myth: every vibration mode radiates sound equally well. Actually a breathing mode, pulsing in phase across its whole surface, radiates far more efficiently.
Myth: a ducking delay is just a quieter delay. It listens - echoes step back while you sing and rise in the gaps, so the repeats never clutter.
Myth: a bigger amplifier is riskier for speakers than a small clipped one. Actually the small clipped amp can be worse, adding harmful high-frequency energy.
The myth: recording extra quiet is the safe choice. Actually too-low gain adds noise you'll amplify later - level should sit strong and clean, not just safe.
Common belief: 6.02N + 1.76 dB gives exact noise for any signal. Actually it's a model built on a full-scale sine — it breaks down for quiet material.
Studio myth: top and bottom snare mics can just both go up. Facing each other, they partly cancel - flip the bottom mic's polarity or the snare thins out.
Common belief: dynamic consistency and dynamic range mean the same thing. Actually consistency is how even a level stays, not the span between quiet and loud.
Myth: setting a mastering limiter's ceiling at 0 dBFS keeps you safe. Actually inter-sample peaks can still exceed that, so ceilings sit near -1 dBTP.
The myth: if the DAW meter reads just under 0 dBFS, the export is safe. Actually that can still hide inter-sample true-peak overs that clip on playback.
Myth: running limiters constantly is free extra loudness. Actually continuous limiting removes transient detail and flattens the mix while stressing drivers.
Myth: boosting lots of EQ bands makes broadcast audio sound better. Actually it eats headroom and invites clipping - corrective cuts usually serve it better.
Myth: 0 is just 0. On a VU meter 0 is a nominal reference; on a digital meter 0 dBFS is the hard ceiling, roughly 18-20 dB above it.
A free-field measurement mic seems like it should work anywhere. Point it off-axis or into a diffuse field and its calibrated flatness no longer holds.
Myth: a driver's mechanical and electrical damping simply add together. Actually Qts combines Qms and Qes in parallel, not by direct addition.
The myth: sample rate and bit depth alone set a session's data rate. Actually channel count multiplies in too - stereo needs twice mono's throughput.
Myth: a MIDI cable carries audio. Actually it only carries performance data like notes and velocity - an instrument must still turn it into sound.
